Just last month, the European policing agency (Europol) had warned that museum thefts across Europe were growing increasingly brazen.And just days before the Renoir heist, internationally known art detective Arthur Brand predicted to the BBC that more high-profile burglaries were likely - particularly in the wake of the successful robbery at the Louvre in Paris last October.The audacious crime in one of the world's most famous museums stunned France, and the stolen jewellery worth €88m (£75m) has still not been recovered, nearly a year on."We will see more of this," says Brand, "because if you are able to hit the Louvre, thieves all around the world are watching that, thinking, 'Wow' - and then they think, 'Don't we have a local museum with gold and silver?'".Within hours of the Louvre burglary, thieves had raided coins from a smaller museum in France. Since then, criminals have stolen a diamond necklace in Vienna, Bronze Age artefacts in Spain, and art from two Italian museums - and that's only what the BBC has written about. The heist at the Renoir Museum in Cagnes-sur-Mer is the latest, and detectives are still working to track down the remaining multi-million-pound paintings - two of which were quickly recovered after thieves dropped them in the museum garden.

articles.title: When an avalanche killed climber Nirmal Purja, his friends faced the hardest mission of all
articles.excerpt: When an avalanche killed climber Nirmal Purja, his friends faced the hardest mission of allFigure caption, Watch: Mingma G recalls the climb to bring home the bodies of his friendsByCarrie DaviesPakistan correspondentReporting fromIslamabadAs he picked his way past the frozen slope towards two bodies, Mingma Gyalje Sherpa knew his friends were gone.Together, the three of them had climbed the world's highest peaks, under crisp mountain skies and in treacherous snowstorms. Nirmal Purja and Kili Pemba Sherpa were two of the strongest climbers Mingma G had ever known.But this July, an avalanche swept through Pakistan's Broad Peak while the two were on their way up, engulfing everything in its path.The drone images seemed clear: no-one had survived.And yet, as Mingma G came closer to the fluorescent down suits, sharp against the snow, he couldn't shake the idea they were waiting for him."I told them: 'It's ok. You don't have to be here in the cold anymore.'"Speaking to the BBC in Islamabad, he recalls the terrible moment he reached for their bodies.Holding one of them, he promised: "I'm here to take you guys home."Image source, Mingma GImage caption, Mingma G embarked on a difficult journey after learning his good friends had diedMingma G and Nirmal Purja met in Pakistan in 2021, where they were part of the first team to summit the world's second-highest mountain, K2, during winter.Mingma G knew of Nirmal - or Nims, as he was known - from his Netflix documentary 14 Peaks, in which he successfully climbed the world's 14 highest mountains in just over six months.The pair, both avid climbers from Nepal, had taken different paths.Mingma G came from the Sherpa community and built his reputation as a mountain guide over 20 years.

articles.title: Céline Dion fans prepare for comeback concert in Paris
articles.excerpt: Céline Dion greeted fans today as she left her hotel, hours before she kicked off her comeback concert in Paris. The Canadian singer returns to the stage on Saturday for her first full concert in six years, to open a sell-out Paris residency after a battle with a rare neurological disorder put a pause in her career. Some fans arrived as early as 06:00 to get a spot in front of LeRoyal Monceau hotel to catch a glimpse of the star before she left. She is one of the best-selling music artists of all time and is due to perform a series of 26 concerts over the next eight months.Read more: Céline Dion announces comeback shows: 'I'm so ready for this'

articles.title: How global trade and oil prices could be hit by Houthi advance
articles.excerpt: Fighters from the Iran-backed Houthi group have seized territory close to the Bab al-Mandab Strait in the Red Sea - a key trade gateway that links Asia and Europe. Houthis have said they pose no threat to international shipping but have reiterated their intention to target vessels from Saudi Arabia.Saudi Arabia has increasingly relied on the Red Sea for oil exports since the US and Israel's war effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz.At least 46,000 people have been displaced in Yemen since fighting escalated last week, according to the United Nations.BBC Verify's Thomas Copeland reports.Produced by Aisha Sembhi. Graphics by Mark Edwards.

articles.title: Has Trump won over voters with his midterm convention?
articles.excerpt: Republicans gathered in Dallas for the closing day of the party's first-ever convention held in the middle of a US presidential term, where US President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance spoke to voters.The aim of the convention was to boost enthusiasm among supporters, even as protesters of Trump gathered outside.The BBC's North America editor Sarah Smith breaks down the main takeaways from the two day event.

articles.title: Watch: Americans remember what they were doing on 9/11
articles.excerpt: On Tuesday 11 September 2001, hijackers seized US passenger jets and crashed them into two New York skyscrapers, killing thousands of people.A third plane destroyed the western face of the Pentagon - the giant headquarters of the US military just outside the nation's capital, Washington DC.The fourth plane crashed in a field in Pennsylvania after passengers fought back. It is thought the hijackers had meant to attack Washington's Capitol Building.The BBC spoke to Americans in Washington about what they were doing on that day and how 9/11 has changed the country.Video by Meiying Wu

articles.title: Brother of Muslim police cadet killed in 9/11 'disappointed' by calls for Mamdani to sit out memorial
articles.excerpt: This year’s 25th anniversary of the September 11th attacks has become embroiled in divisive politics. There are controversial calls for the city’s first Muslim Mayor to sit out the commemorative event, including from Rudy Giuliani who was New York’s mayor on the morning of 9/11.Mayor Zohran Mamdani has said he will attend and his focus will be on the families who lost loved ones.Zeshan Hamdani lost his older brother Salman, a Muslim American New York police cadet, in the North Tower. He spoke to the BBC's Nada Tawfik over his thoughts on this anniversary.Video filmed and edited by Andrew Blum; produced by Pratiksha Ghildial

articles.title: Drone display recreates the Twin Towers over New York City
articles.excerpt: According to organisers, 2,977 drones recreated the Twin Towers at full scale with each light representing a victim of the 9/11 attacks. The artwork, titled "2,977 Lights Over New York Harbor", is a commemorative public art installation in collaboration with artists, producers, and members of the 9/11 community, including victims' families, survivors, and first responders.SubsectionUS & CanadaPublished2 days agoRelated topicsSeptember 11 attacksNew York CityUnited StatesDrones

articles.title: Burial of King Oyo takes place in Uganda as news anchor prepares for throne
articles.excerpt: Uganda’s King Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV, long the world’s youngest monarch, has been buried among the tombs of his royal forebears as ⁠his Tooro kingdom looked to put ⁠a bitter succession battle behind ​it.Oyo’s appointed successor, the news anchor Edward Rukidi Kijanangoma, cast nine coffee berries into the grave at the Karambi Royal Tombs, marking the formal handover of power in the western Ugandan kingdom.Oyo made global headlines in 1995 when he took the throne at the age of three. Images of the toddler king wearing a crown and royal robes sparked curiosity and adoration around the world.King Oyo of the Toro kingdom was for a long time the world’s youngest monarch. Photograph: Sipa/ShutterstockHe died last month at 34 ⁠in the United States, where he was receiving treatment for cancer.Uganda is led by an elected head of state but retains several kingdoms that pre-date the ​British colonial era and are regarded as bulwarks of traditional identity ‌and heritage.At a church service before ‌the burial, Oyo, who became a UN goodwill ambassador championing the fight against HIV and Aids, was eulogised as a reserved but jovial young man.“Although ‌he became king and carried responsibilities far beyond what most people ever experience, he never completely lost the young boy who loved to have fun,” said his sister, Ruth Komuntale.Royal guards clad in orange shawls then led the hearse carrying Oyo’s casket through the streets of the kingdom’s capital, Fort Portal, to the royal tombs, as thousands of mourners joined the procession on foot.The burial, which was held 31 years to the day after Oyo’s coronation, followed days of bickering within the notoriously fractious royal family.A committee consisting of members ‌of the royal clan announced on Wednesday it had chosen Oyo’s cousin, Kijanangoma, a news anchor and editor at state broadcaster UBC, as king.But the late king’s immediate family said his hitherto unknown son should succeed him, as called ​for in his will.

articles.title: Six Nigerians extradited to US over $6m online romance scam
articles.excerpt: Six Nigerian nationals linked to an organized criminal network that allegedly swindled American women out of more than $6m through online romance scams were extradited to the United States on Friday.South African police confirmed they were to be extradited earlier on Friday, while local news in Africa confirmed that the Directorate for Priority Crime Investigation, known as the Hawks, facilitated their handover to officials from the US Federal Bureau of Investigation and Secret Service at Cape Town international airport, in collaboration with Interpol South Africa.The men, who were arrested in the South African city of Cape Town in 2021, face wire fraud and money laundering charges.They are accused of belonging to a criminal network known as the Black Axe, which Interpol describes as being among criminal groups responsible for a significant share of the world’s cyber-enabled financial fraud, typically through romance, cryptocurrency and investment scams.According to South African police, the men are alleged to have targeted more than 100 women in the US, defrauding them of more than $6m through online romance or love scams.Among the alleged victims were pensioners and businesspeople who were reportedly targeted through sophisticated online relationships.“Through the coordination of Interpol South Africa, the six will today be transported from a correctional facility in Cape Town to Cape Town international airport, where they will be handed over to officials from the FBI and the United States Secret Service, who arrived in South Africa this morning,” said police spokesperson Katlego Mogale.A recent operation by Interpol targeting west African organized crime groups led to the arrest of 58 people and the identification of 263 suspects linked to various criminal networks involved in similar crimes, the multinational police body said last month.The operation aimed to disrupt money laundering, identify high-value targets, seize assets, and support arrests and

articles.title: $15m fund launched to create ‘unstoppable momentum’ to end FGM worldwide
articles.excerpt: Frontline activists and leaders in the fight against female genital mutilation, which has affected more than 230 million women and girls worldwide, have welcomed an unprecedented $15.5m (£11.4m) fund aimed at creating “unstoppable momentum” to finally end the practice.The launch of the fund comes as women’s rights are increasingly under attack and donor funding is in sharp decline, particularly for work led by FGM survivors in local communities. It is thought to be the largest single philanthropic contribution to ending the practice of FGM.The United Nations has set a goal of elimination by by 2030, but progress is not on track as funding declines and legal protections are challenged.Funding received by the largest initiative to end the practice – a joint programme operated in 18 countries by the UN’s sexual and reproductive health agency, UNFPA, and the UN humanitarian organisation for children, Unicef – fell by 45% last year, from $29.6m to $16.3m.The Her Horizon Fund has been seeded with $14m from the Wallace Global Fund, plus an additional $1.5m contribution from an anonymous donor, making $15.5m in total.The aim of Her Horizon Fund, set up by the US-based Wallace Global Fund, is to pool $100m from donors to reach a “tipping point” towards ending FGM within a generation.Ifrah Ahmed, a Somali-Irish activist and survivor of FGM who set up the Ifrah Foundation to end practice in Somalia, where it is nearly universal, said: “By giving $14m, the global fund will ensure activists can continue their work in this area.”UN funding worth $300,000 to her organisation was cut by UNFPA last year, but Ahmed managed to raise money from elsewhere.

articles.title: Secret son revelation ignites bitter succession dispute in Ugandan kingdom
articles.excerpt: A traditional Ugandan kingdom has become engulfed in a bitter succession dispute after the family of a king who recently died rejected the selection of a television news anchor as his successor.King Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV, who became the world’s youngest reigning monarch when he took the throne in the kingdom of Tooro in 1995 at the age of three, died on 27 August in the US, where he was receiving cancer treatment.King Oyo Nyimba, aged 13, sits between his mother Best Kemigisha and an unidentified adviser during celebrations marking his first decade in power in Fort Portal, Uganda. Photograph: ReutersOn Wednesday, the royal clan’s succession committee announced it had chosen Oyo’s cousin Prince Edward Rukidi Kijanangoma, a news anchor and editor at the public broadcaster UBC, as crown prince.However, at a press conference held later the same day, Oyo’s sister, Princess Ruth Nsemere Komuntale, said that according to her brother’s will, a son whose existence had not been publicly known until his death should succeed him.Princess Ruth Komuntale waiting to receive the body of her brother, the late King Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV, at Entebbe International airport last week. Photograph: Hajarah Nalwadda/Getty ImagesThe kingdom’s ‌spokesperson shared a section of the document, which says: “I hereby declare and direct that if, at the date of my death, I am survived by a son lawfully recognised as my biological son, I appoint him as my heir to the throne of the kingdom of Tooro.”In a statement on Thursday, Oyo’s mother, Queen Mother Best Kemigisa Akiiki, denounced a “self-appointed group of clan members” who had selected a new king despite having had the will read to them hours earlier.She also claimed that the royal family had been put under house arrest. Troops had “removed the royal guards without notice, and ... were deployed around the palace,” she said.

articles.title: Uganda to withdraw from Invictus Games ‘out of respect for King Charles’, says military chief
articles.excerpt: Uganda is withdrawing from the Duke of Sussex’s Invictus Games, the country’s military chief has said, out of respect for King Charles amid division over the “Harry-Meghan nonsense”.Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba, son of the Ugandan president, made the surprise announcement in a post on X on Wednesday.Kainerugaba wrote: “In order not to be construed as being opposed to His Majesty King Charles III of the United Kingdom, whom we deeply revere, Uganda hereby withdraws from the Invictus Games. We shall not participate in anything that does not have His Majesty’s approval.”The timing of the post suggests it may be in response to an official letter to UK senior government and military officials on behalf of Charles that reiterated the Duke and Duchess of Sussex were not working royals and would not use their HRH styles.When asked by the Times about what had motivated the move, Kainerugaba is reported to have said: “I have factions in the Ministry of Defence that support that Harry-Meghan nonsense. I had to quash it straight away. I support the monarch. Period.”The news, first reported by the Uganda Pulse news website, will be a blow to Harry, who two months ago stood alongside Uganda’s defence minister, Kiryowa Kiwanuka, at an Invictus Games event in London to announce that the East African nation would be the 26th country to enter the multisport event for wounded service personnel.At the time, Kiwanuka praised the Ugandan president, Yoweri Museveni for his “visionary leadership” and Kainerugaba, a Sandhurst graduate, for “championing our team’s entry”, adding that their support “marks a new chapter for our servicemen and women”.The Ugandan government spokesperson Alan Kasujja confirmed to the BBC: “Gen Kainerugaba decides whether or not the UPDF [Uganda People’s Defence Force] participates in the Invictus Games. What you saw is his stated position.

articles.title: Canada offers air defense support for Ukraine as Zelenskyy visits
articles.excerpt: Canada offered support on Thursday to boost Ukraine’s air defenses and help replenish its drone stocks, as the countries pledged to deepen their alliance during a visit by Volodymyr Zelenskyy.Mark Carney hosted the president of Ukraine in Calgary in the western province of Alberta, where the Canadian prime minister grew up among a large community of people with Ukrainian heritage.“Canada will always be with you,” Carney assured Zelenskyy.The leaders signed an agreement to work toward a “hundred-year partnership”.That deal, to be negotiated over the coming months, aims to codify cooperation in a range of areas, including defense, critical minerals and energy.“Our two nations have been connected since 1893,” Carney said, referring to a wave of Ukrainians who migrated to the new Canadian nation.In Alberta, there are an estimated 350,000 Canadians of Ukrainian descent.“Ukrainians helped build Canada and Canadians will help rebuild Ukraine,” Carney said.The support announced on Thursday includes C$350m (US$253m) provided through the United States’ Joint Ukraine Multinational Program – Services, Training and Articles Rapid Timeline (Jumpstart) program.Zelenskyy has emphasized the need for increased air defense as Russia ramps up ballistic missile attacks.Carney said Canada was also offering C$450m in loan guarantees to enhance the Ukrainian energy supply.The funds will help repair damaged infrastructure, increase storage capacity and improve power supply to hospitals.Carney said the goal of the energy support was “to help Ukrainians get through the winter”, a difficult period when the country endures rolling blackouts amid often frigid temperatures.Canada is moving aggressively to increase its own drone stocks, Carney said, announcing a deal that will see 30% of new Canadian production head to Ukraine.Zelenskyy told reporters that “these drones will go to Ukraine immediately to [the] battlefield, immediately to our people, our soldiers … to save our children, our

articles.title: Rubio signals shift to working with allies to fight drug trade as latest boat strike kills three
articles.excerpt: The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, gave new clarity on the approach toward combating drug trafficking in Latin American waters, saying the Trump administration was focused on working with allied countries and aligning with their laws but insisted the military would “still blow up ships if need be”.The public acknowledgment of a shift in US strategy comes a year after Washington began a campaign of unilateral deadly strikes against those it calls “narco-terrorists” operating boats in international waters.Late Wednesday, US Southern Command announced the latest such strike in the Caribbean Sea, saying it killed three people. That brought the number of people who have been killed in boat strikes by the US military to at least 230 in 69 strikes.Still, the Trump administration is focused on building agreements for joint operations with allied countries in the region, including Colombia and Ecuador, that comply with their laws in their waters.“I think its an incredible advance for the first time to have countries that are willing to participate in these efforts in their territorial waters,” Rubio told reporters on a trip to the Ecuadorian capital, Quito.“The important point is that these routes are being disrupted. These routes are being ended,” he added.He said the decision is “a strike-by-strike or operation-by-operation determination” that depends on the threat and location of the boat.Recent US interdictions in Latin American waters are unlike the Trump administration’s initial strikes on alleged drug-trafficking boats that began in September 2025. People onboard floating refueling stations said to be supporting drug trafficking have been removed and transferred to Ecuadorian authorities.

articles.title: Notorious Ecuadorian crime gang designated a terrorist group by US
articles.excerpt: The US has designated Ecuador’s Los Tiguerones gang, which stormed a television station during a live broadcast in 2024, as a terrorist organisation as the Trump administration expands its campaign against narcotics traffickers it says are destabilising Latin America.The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, made the announcement in Quito, where he met Ecuadorian president Daniel Noboa, one of several rightwing allies of Donald Trump whom Rubio is courting as a security partner during a three-nation tour through Latin America that began on Tuesday.Rubio said the Los Tiguerones gang was linked to narcotics trafficking, as well as attacks on civilians, law enforcement officers and journalists.“We are not talking about an ordinary mafia, nor are we talking about common criminals, we are talking about terrorists who, in many cases, possess weapons and equipment resembling the national armies of certain countries,” he said.The heavily armed gang’s attack on the TC Televisión network in 2024 prompted Noboa to declare a state of “internal armed conflict”, amid claims foreign drug gangs had descended on Ecuador to take control of important routes for coca grown in neighbouring Colombia and Peru and then shipped to the US.Live footage from the El Noticiero news programme showed men toting pistols, shotguns, machine guns, grenades and sticks of dynamite.

articles.title: Family of British man found dead in Grenada ask local police to work with UK investigators
articles.excerpt: The family of a British father who was found dead in the Caribbean in January is urging authorities in Grenada to work with UK police to uncover the truth about his death.Andrew Frederick’s body was found in the property he was staying at in Grenada on 4 January. An autopsy, performed in the same week by a privately hired pathologist, concluded that the 47-year-old’s death was a homicide.In June, Grenada’s director of public prosecution, Howard Pinnock, said at a press conference that Frederick’s and another pending case would be sent to the coroner to determine the cause of death “because there is no basis in terms of both investigations that any homicide has occurred”.After a sustained campaign by the family, British authorities became involved and Frederick’s body was repatriated to the UK last month, where a second autopsy was carried out.The UK coroner has noted that Frederick’s organs are missing and the death is currently “unascertained”.At the start of an inquest at West London coroner’s court last week, senior coroner Lydia Brown said the Metropolitan police are now investigating Frederick’s death.The family, who attended the court hearing by video link, said the coroner’s “decision to suspend Andrew’s inquest to allow the Metropolitan police to conduct a criminal investigation marks a significant turning point”.In statement to the Guardian, they urged Grenada and the UK to work together to find out what happened to Frederick.“We are encouraged and grateful that the Metropolitan police investigation is now under way. Justice for Andrew depends on everyone with the power to act, on both sides of the Atlantic, doing what is right,” the statement said.It added: “Andrew was a deeply loved member of a close-knit family; a son, brother, father and grandson.

articles.title: ‘It’s hell’: father of slain Australian surfers tells Mexico homicide trial about identifying sons’ bodies
articles.excerpt: The father of two Australian surfers killed in Mexico two years ago testified in court on Tuesday that his life had been turned into hell, as the high-profile trial continued into its second day.Three men are charged in the killing of Australian brothers Jake and Callum Robinson, aged 30 and 33, respectively, and their 30-year-old American friend Jack Carter Rhoad, who were on a surfing trip to Mexico’s Pacific coast in April 2024.Authorities say the three were killed in an attempted robbery, and their bodies were found dumped in a cliff-top shaft with gunshot wounds to their heads.“It’s hell,” the victims’ father Martin Robinson told the court. “It’s hard for a parent to lose a son, and we lost two sons.”“It’s not just the loss, but also the potential they had the dreams that lay ahead of them, the places they travelled, and the love they had for others,” he said.Robinson described the ordeal of having to identify his sons’ bodies: Callum by a tattoo on his forearm, while identifying Jake was more difficult and required photographs.Rhoad’s mother Page compared the crime to an execution.“I miss my son every day, and I don’t know if I will ever be able to regain my balance,” she testified. “Carter loved Mexico. He spoke fluent Spanish and loved dancing, Mexican food and its people.”Authorities say the men were killed during an attempt to steal their pickup truck, which was later found burned near their bodies.A protected witness testified Monday that they accompanied one of the defendants to the crime scene and fled after hearing gunshots, and were later threatened into silence.The surfers’ disappearances and deaths sparked widespread outrage and grief in Australia and the United States, prompting a major social media search for their bodies.“We hold no resentment toward the people who did this, but we cannot understand how they could have taken the lives of two beautiful people,” Martin Robinson told the court.The trial is expected to run until the end of September.

articles.title: Xi Jinping gets red carpet at Brics summit amid thaw in India-China relations
articles.excerpt: The Chinese president, Xi Jinping, has received a red-carpet welcome in India for a summit of Brics developing nations, as regional rivals Beijing and Delhi make a public display of thawing relations while quietly competing to lead at a time of shaky US global dominance.As Xi stepped off the plane, he was walked past an honour guard of Indian soldiers and traditional dancers in colourful dresses. Later on Saturday, he was due to attend a gala dinner for the two-day summit.The Russian president, Vladimir Putin, and Iranian president, Masoud Pezeshkian, had already been welcomed by the Indian prime minister, Narendra Modi, who is hosting one of the group’s most closely watched gatherings since its inception.The summit marks Xi’s first visit to India in seven years and is seen as the biggest step towards reconciliation after a deadly 2020 military clash along the disputed Himalayan border, in which ‌20 Indian and four Chinese soldiers were killed.Ties between the nuclear-armed Asian giants have been warming recently, with flights and high-level contacts gradually being restored. China was “willing” to work with India to properly manage differences and be “good neighbours and friends”, China’s foreign ministry said on Friday.Leaders and diplomats have been convening in India for the annual gathering of the Brics grouping, named after five of its earliest members – Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa – that was conceived as a counterweight to western dominance.This summit comes as wars in Ukraine and the Middle East, along with rising US-China tensions, test the bloc’s ability to find common ground.Since its inception in 2009, Brics has expanded as a forum for major emerging economies to include Egypt, Ethiopia, Indonesia, Iran, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates (UAE).

articles.title: Death toll from Philippines ferry fire rises to 35, as officials warn toll will grow
articles.excerpt: The bodies of passengers killed in a ferry fire off the Philippines arrived at a port near the resort town of Coron, Palawan, on Saturday morning, as the country’s coast guard warned the death toll of 35 would grow.Tents were being set up to receive 30 bodies brought from the M/V June Aster, which ran aground near the tourist hotspot after a fire erupted on Wednesday evening and tore through the vessel “in seconds”.Coast guard spokesperson Noemie Cayabyab told a Saturday press conference the remains would be turned over to police forensic investigators for “proper disposition and identification” before allowing local authorities to inform family members.“Currently, we are focused on the retrieval, and after that we will proceed with the investigation,” she said, confirming the bodies had been found in the ship’s economy accommodation area.Police investigators were seen arriving at the port shortly after the press conference ended.Asked how many bodies remained aboard the ship, she said authorities would provide an update later in the day.Cayabyab told AFP on Friday evening that the first transfer had been capped at 30 bodies because of the capacity of the patrol vessel transporting them and that additional cadavers remained on the ferry.Five others had been confirmed dead in the immediate wake of the fire.Photos released by the coast guard showed rows of body bags being placed into a small ship alongside men in hazmat suits. Thirty passengers and 13 crew have so far been rescued, while 54 people remain unaccounted for.On Friday, Cayabyab had told a radio station the fire had begun in the cargo hold, then tore through the ship within seconds.“From the time that they heard the loud explosion, the appearance of smoke, and then fire.

articles.title: Buddhist monk arrested in Thailand on suspicion of embezzling $2.8m
articles.excerpt: Police in Thailand have arrested a senior Buddhist monk on suspicion of embezzling $2.8m intended for his monastery, alongside a suspected female accomplice he was filmed having sex with.The case is the latest scandal to hit the clergy in the Buddhist-majority country, after a sex and extortion case involving senior monks last year prompted public outrage and calls for greater scrutiny of temple finances.Phra Wachirayan Wi, the 66-year-old abbot of the 14th-century temple Wat Phutthaisawan in the ancient capital of Ayutthaya, was arrested on Thursday on charges including embezzlement and money laundering, according to the lead police investigator Pattanasak Bupphasuwan.A 47-year-old woman accused of helping convert and conceal the money was also arrested.Leaked CCTV footage of the pair having sex on a table in the monk’s residence was widely broadcast on Thai media.In Thailand, Buddhist monks take a vow of celibacy and also renounce material possessions.Police began investigating Phra Wachirayan in mid-July after receiving an anonymous tip alleging him of misconduct and misuse of temple funds.Pattanasak, a commander of the police crime suppression division, said investigators identified two streams of money linked to donation receipts issued in the temple’s name.About 89m baht ($2.7m or £2m) was donated for temple renovations, with another 2.8m baht in payments for Buddhist amulets and other sacred objects, he said.“But the money from both streams did not enter the temple’s account – not a single baht,” Pattanasak told a news conference on Friday.Police say authorities seized assets worth about 215m baht, including 16kg of gold bars, jewellery, watches and land title deeds Photograph: Panumas Sanguanwong/Thai News Pix/AFP/Getty ImagesHe said authorities had seized assets worth about 215m baht, including 16kg (35lb) of gold bars and jewellery and 28 land title deeds.Police are investigating which are personal property and which belong to the temple.“We will expand

articles.title: Japan seeks change to new UN world map over Russia 'misconception'
articles.excerpt: Japan has asked for the revision of a new world map adopted by the UN because it said it made the disputed Kuril islands appear to belong to Russia.The UN general assembly voted on Friday to adopt the new map, which makes the African continent larger while also shrinking North America and Europe, drawing condemnation from the US.Japan was among the 164 UN members that supported the resolution, but has now taken issue with it because it shows the Kurils, known in Japan as the Northern Territories, in the same colour as Russia.Ukraine last week abstained in the UN vote on the map as it showed occupied Crimea in a different colour to the rest of the country, which its representatives at the UN warned opens a “Pandora’s box” violating the UN charter and international law.Japanese government spokesperson Minoru Kihara on Thursday said the new map – known as the Equal Earth cartographic projection – “contained a depiction contradicting the Japanese government’s position”.“We lodged a protest with the map site’s operator through our diplomatic channel to demand the correction of this depiction,” Kihara told reporters.He declined to say when the issue was brought to government’s attention but said Japan “needs to prevent misconceptions of our territories and geographical names from spreading”.The disputed islands were seized in 1945 by the former Soviet Union, which then expelled the Japanese population.The disputed Kuril islands, top right.

articles.title: Wall Street Journal publisher convicted in Hong Kong of deterring reporter from union role
articles.excerpt: A Hong Kong court has convicted the publisher of the Wall Street Journal of deterring a reporter from taking up a trade union role, in a case that raised concerns about press freedom in the city.The newspaper dismissed Selina Cheng just weeks after she was appointed chair of the Hong Kong Journalist Association (HKJA) in 2024. She was told at the time her termination was officially due to restructuring.Outside court on Thursday, Cheng said: “If reporters’ employment rights are not sufficiently safeguarded, or when their rights are violated and not enforced in law, then we can no longer work safely as reporters.”Principal magistrate David Cheung ruled that Dow Jones Publishing, the parent company of the Wall Street journal, was guilty of “preventing or deterring an employee from exercising trade union rights,” but acquitted it of “dismissing or discriminating against an employee because she exercised those rights.”Cheng, who covered China’s automobiles and energy sectors for the WSJ, said her editor had told her that employees should not be seen as advocating for press freedom in “places like Hong Kong”, saying it could be perceived as a conflict of interest. She alleged her employer had attempted to prevent her from taking up a role in the union.She said the company told her that she needed to seek the firm’s approval for outside activities and requested her to leave her then-board position at the association.Cheng launched the private prosecution against Dow Jones Publishing after losing her job in July 2024, weeks after taking up the position as chair of the union.The company pleaded not guilty to both charges, which each carry a maximum fine of HK$100,000 (about $12,750).Sentencing is expected to be handed down at a later date.During the trial, the defence argued that Cheng was terminated because of redundancy and that the prosecution had not sufficiently proved that the firm’s management instructed Cheng’s supervisor.

articles.title: NSW to put strict caps on screen time in classrooms while pushing for ‘pen and paper’ learning
articles.excerpt: The New South Wales government has announced it will implement limits on screen time in public school classrooms and push for students to take part in daily “pen and paper” learning.The state’s new regulations follow a similar announcement from the Victorian government and suggestions by the federal education minister, Jason Clare, that students might need a “digital detox”.Under the new regulations, Kindergarten to Year 2 students will be restricted to 15 minutes per day of learning on individual student devices, such as tablets or laptops.Older children will be allowed additional time: up to 30 minutes a day for students in Years 3 and 4; and 45 minutes for Years 5 and 6. Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here High school students will have restrictions based on their individual subject. In Years 7 to 10, the use of personal digital devices will be limited to a quarter of subject time; senior high school students will be allowed to use devices for up to half their learning time.The government also says there would be new guidelines that limit the use of screens for homework, including not recommending any such use for children younger than Year 5.Marcia Langton says schools teaching about racism must take care not to traumatise children – videoGuidelines will also recommend “a minimum of one hour a day” be devoted to pen and paper learning.The screen limits will be recommended next year and become mandatory in NSW schools from 2028.The state’s education minister, Prue Car, said the government’s research “is telling us that excessive screen use is a problem”.
articles.summary: 新南威尔士州政府宣布，将对公立学校课堂上的屏幕使用时间实施限制，并推动学生每天进行「纸笔」学习。该州新规出台之前，维多利亚州政府已发布类似公告，联邦教育部长杰森·克莱尔也提出学生可能需要进行一次「数字排毒」。根据新规，幼儿园至二年级的学生每天在平板电脑或笔记本电脑等个人学生设备上学习的时间将被限制在15分钟以内。年龄较大的儿童可获额外时间：三、四年级学生每天最多30分钟，五、六年级学生为45分钟。高中学生将根据各自科目受到限制。七至十年级使用个人数字设备的时间将被限制在学科课时的四分之一以内；高中高年级学生则最多可将设备用于一半的学习时间。政府还表示，将出台新指南限制用屏幕做作业，包括不建议五年级以下儿童以任何此类方式完成作业。指南还将建议「每天至少一小时」用于纸笔学习。这些屏幕使用限制将于明年起作为建议推行，并从2028年起在新南威尔士州各校强制执行。该州教育部长普鲁·卡尔表示，政府的研究「告诉我们，过度使用屏幕是一个问题」。

articles.title: News live: Albanese hits back at Hanson criticism of his mother’s use of public housing; Melissa Doyle appointed Australia Day council chair
articles.excerpt: From 2h agoHanson ‘started a fight, and I intend to win it’, Hastie saysKrishani DhanjiIt’s the fight that dominated parliament this week – and is still going – with Andrew Hastie this morning challenging Pauline Hanson to explain her stance on executing prisoners on the battlefield.A brief recap: Hastie has this week feuded with the One Nation leader over a cartoon video by the party released in late July that calls the former SAS captain a “traitor” after he gave evidence against Ben Roberts-Smith in his failed defamation trial.Hastie then called Hanson a “lying coward” and “weak and glass jawed” for not taking ownership of the animated cartoon (she claimed she hadn’t called Hastie a traitor) or removing it from her social media.Speaking to News24 this morning, Hastie says Roberts-Smith deserves a fair trial and the presumption of innocence in a separate criminal case currently before the courts.Zooming out to the political battle, Hastie says he’ll continue the fight with Hanson and One Nation – who have announced they will target his seat of Canning in Western Australia. double quotation markI’ve copped it for the last six months, and sometimes you just got to draw a line in the sand, because weakness is provocative. People want strength. These guys thought I was weak … I’ve always been respectful of Pauline. I’ve tried to build a relationship with her in the past, and it’s been good. And then she came for me and I started to see, OK, this is not the person I thought she was. And now she’s my political opponent, and she started a fight, and I intend to win it.
articles.summary: 2小时前：哈斯蒂称，汉森「挑起了一场争斗，我打算赢下它」。这是本周主导议会、且仍在持续的争斗——安德鲁·哈斯蒂今早要求保琳·汉森解释其关于在战场上处决俘虏的立场。简要回顾：本周，哈斯蒂与单一民族党领袖发生争执，起因是该党7月底发布的一段卡通视频。此前哈斯蒂在本·罗伯茨-史密斯的诽谤案败诉中作证指控对方，该视频随即将这位前SAS上尉称为「叛徒」。哈斯蒂随后称汉森是「撒谎的懦夫」，「软弱、玻璃下巴」，因为她既不承认拥有这段动画视频（她声称自己从未称哈斯蒂为叛徒），也不将其从社交媒体上删除。哈斯蒂今早对News24表示，罗伯茨-史密斯理应获得公正审判，并在目前法院正在审理的另一宗刑事案件中享有无罪推定。放眼这场政治斗争，哈斯蒂表示他将继续与汉森及单一民族党较量——后者已宣布将在西澳大利亚州瞄准他的坎宁选区。他说：「过去六个月我一直承受着攻击，有时你就是得划下一条底线，因为软弱是会招致挑衅的。人们想要强硬。这些人以为我软弱……我一直尊重保琳。过去我试图与她建立关系，而且一直不错。然后她冲我来了，我开始看清，好吧，这不是我以为的那个人。现在她是我的政治对手，她挑起了一场争斗，我打算赢下它。」

articles.title: Andrew Hastie vows to go ‘all the way’ in Pauline Hanson fight as Joyce denies ‘buyers’ remorse’ claim
articles.excerpt: Andrew Hastie has vowed to go “all the way” in his fight with Pauline Hanson, as he suggested One Nation MPs Barnaby Joyce and David Farley were likely feeling buyers’ remorse for joining the party.The Liberal MP and former SAS captain repeated his accusation that Hanson was a “lying coward” on Sunday, after she continued to refuse to take down an animated cartoon that described Hastie as a “traitor”. This came after he was subpoenaed to give evidence during Ben Roberts-Smith’s failed defamation trial.“She’s still a lying coward. I’m not backing down,” Hastie told News24 on Sunday. “I put the challenge to her. She could have accepted that she’d got it wrong and pulled it down, but she refused to do so, and she has doubled down. Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here “As I said to Barnaby in text, I will continue. Consider last week a demonstration. They haven’t seen anything yet.“I’ll go all the way with One Nation if they want … she started a fight, and I intend to win it.”He also said he had previously tried to develop a relationship with Hanson, but that she is “not the person I thought she was”.Back to Back Barries: Andrew Hastie v Pauline Hanson – videoHastie accepted Joyce’s apology to him over the cartoon video on Friday, who claimed he had not seen it. But the Liberal MP claimed his colleague, and One Nation MP David Farley, were likely having “buyers’ remorse” over joining the party.“The whole party centres on her. I think this is why Barnaby Joyce and I reckon David Farley are probably having buyers’ remorse. They’re thinking, what did I get myself into?” Hastie said.“I’ll say this about Barnaby Joyce. I feel sorry for the bloke, all right?
articles.summary: 安德鲁·哈斯蒂誓言在与保琳·汉森的争斗中「一路走到底」，并暗示一国党议员巴纳比·乔伊斯和大卫·法利很可能对加入该党感到「买家懊悔」。这位自由党议员、前SAS上尉周日再次指责汉森是「撒谎的懦夫」，此前她继续拒绝撤下一段将哈斯蒂描述为「叛徒」的动画短片。此前，他因本·罗伯茨-史密斯的诽谤案败诉而被传唤作证。哈斯蒂周日对News24表示：「她仍然是个撒谎的懦夫。我不会退缩。我向她发出了挑战。她本可以承认自己搞错了并撤下视频，但她拒绝这么做，反而变本加厉。」「正如我在短信中对巴纳比所说，我会继续下去。把上周当作一次演示。他们还没见识到真正的厉害。」「如果一国党想打，我会奉陪到底……是她挑起了这场争斗，我打算赢下它。」他还表示，自己此前曾试图与汉森建立关系，但她「不是我以为的那个人」。哈斯蒂于周五接受了乔伊斯就那段卡通视频向他作出的道歉，乔伊斯声称自己此前没有看过该视频。但这位自由党议员声称，他的同僚、一国党议员大卫·法利很可能对加入该党感到「买家懊悔」。哈斯蒂说：「整个党都围绕着她。我认为这就是为什么巴纳比·乔伊斯——我猜还有大卫·法利——很可能正感到买家懊悔。他们在想，我到底把自己卷进了什么？」「关于巴纳比·乔伊斯，我要说：我同情这家伙，好吗？」

articles.title: Do not call her a racist: anti-Pauline Hanson strategists tell campaigners character attacks won’t work in Victoria
articles.excerpt: The message from strategists was blunt: do not, however tempting, personally attack Pauline Hanson or call her a racist.The request has been made to progressive campaigners and unionists who have been asked to start one-on-one conversations with One Nation supporters before the Victorian election in November.It is also indicative of a strategic rethink in response to One Nation’s sustained surge in public support and the party’s recent wins in state and federal byelections and in South Australia.Separate training sessions run by the peak body for unions in Victoria, the Trades Hall Council, and the progressive campaign group GetUp, have warned members they may be inadvertently pushing people to One Nation by not respectfully engaging with their legitimate economic concerns.“As best as you can, I know it’s hard, don’t make it personal,” a GetUp strategist told hundreds of members on a Thursday night Zoom call.“Going after Pauline Hanson personally and calling her a racist, or going after her character, although very tempting, just confirms what people already believe: that she is an outsider and the establishment is attacking her.”This is a change of approach for the progressive group, which spent hundreds of thousands of dollars on ads personally attacking Hanson and her deputy leader, Barnaby Joyce, during the Farrer byelection. The ads, which linked the pair to Donald Trump, had little impact.

articles.title: Labor has had 12 years to fix Victorian roads. Turning to ‘pothole populism’ now may be too late
articles.excerpt: At a press conference to celebrate the sold-out NFL match played at Melbourne’s MCG on Friday, the Victorian premier, Ben Carroll, was heckled on one issue.“Fix the potholes,” a punter called out as they walked past the Victorian premier’s press conference.No matter where you’re driving in Victoria – be it a rural road, regional freeway or an inner-city street – you’re bound to encounter one. Then comes the split-second decision: swerve into another lane, or power through and hope your tyres survive the impact?For regional Victorians it has been an issue for years. In 2024, the National party began collating images for its “Potholes for All Seasons” calendar, which was distributed to MPs at state parliament last year.But now potholes have become so omnipresent they could become the defining symbol of the Victorian election in November.At the Nepean byelection in May, the opposition leader, Jess Wilson, and her successful candidate, Anthony Marsh, made it a central issue of the campaign – going so far as to fill a pothole themselves, prompting an investigation by the transport department.Allow Instagram content?This article includes content provided by Instagram. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content, click 'Allow and continue'.The headlines have kept coming. In July, the ABC reported that seven cars were forced off the Calder Freeway near Gisborne due to tyre damage from potholes. In August, the Herald Sun reported a dismal 23 Victorian drivers had received compensation from the Transport Accident Commission for pothole damage over the last two years – despite thousands of complaints.AI-generated ads for the political lobby group Fix Victoria feature potholes prominently. On Thursday, the group stood outside Parliament station handing out bumper stickers that read: “Not drunk, avoiding potholes”.

articles.title: Donald Trump says he would ‘love’ to see united Ireland
articles.excerpt: Donald Trump has said he would “love” to see a united Ireland and that it “may as well happen now”.The US president appeared to endorse the push for constitutional change on the island at the start of a two-day visit to Ireland on Saturday. The unexpected intervention prompted a swift rebuttal from the UK government and Northern Ireland’s unionist leaders.“I don’t want ⁠to cause any problems, ​but ‌I will ‌tell you, I’d love ‌to see it unified,” Trump told reporters at joint press conference with the taoiseach, Micheál Martin, in Dublin. “I think it would be a great feather in everybody’s cap if that happened. You know what? The way I look at it, it’s going to happen eventually. It may as well happen now.”The unification of Northern Ireland with the republic of Ireland would be “fantastic”, Trump said. “The UK will have something to say about it, obviously. But I think it would be a great thing. I mean, how can it be bad?”Micheál Martin welcomes Donald Trump to Farmleigh House, in Dublin, during his trip to the Republic of Ireland. Photograph: Ben Birchall/PAThe intervention jolted his hosts and came two weeks after Andy Burnham said a referendum on unification was “off the table”, which angered Sinn Féin and other Irish nationalists.Speaking later on Saturday, Trump acknowledged that his comments on unification, made in response to a reporter’s question, would be controversial. “No matter what you say or how you say it, there’s no good answer,” he said. “I gave a nice answer, I think.

articles.title: Trump says he would ‘love’ to see unified Ireland and ‘it may as well happen now’ as he visits Dublin – as it happened

articles.title: Sweden’s extremely close election could see far right enter government
articles.excerpt: Sweden goes to the polls on Sunday in an extremely close election that could see the far right enter government for the first time if the country’s rightwing parties can form a majority.Opinion polls show the centre-left opposition alliance ahead, with Magdalena ⁠Andersson of the Social Democrats the favourite to become prime minister again after four years in opposition, but her bloc’s lead has narrowed considerably in the final days of the campaign.Magdalena Andersson, the leader of the Social Democrats. Photograph: Simon Johnson/ReutersIn 2022, the current prime minister, Ulf Kristersson, the leader of the centre-right Moderates, broke a longstanding taboo to make a deal with the far-right Sweden Democrats (SD), so that his minority coalition could form a government.That agreement gave the SD outsized influence over government policy, especially on crime and immigration, and Kristersson has now gone further, promising ministerial posts for the SD if he is returned to power.The election comes days after Germany’s nativist Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) seized first place in a state election, and as Marine Le Pen leads the polls for next year’s presidential vote in France.Legal and civil rights experts have warned that such a result could further undermine Sweden’s long-held reputation as a global champion of human rights, which has significantly deteriorated under the current government.“What we have seen in the past four years is huge changes when it comes to policies on crime and immigration,” said John Stauffer, legalthe director at Civil Rights Defenders.Sweden’s prime minister, Ulf Kristersson, talks to members of the media after a Moderate party rally.

articles.title: Firewall compromised: has Friedrich Merz blown ‘democracy’s last shot’?
articles.excerpt: A cataclysm. A 9.0 earthquake. A five-alarm fire. A bitter rejection of Germany’s joyous reunification three decades ago, and a threat to the democratic postwar order.Sizing up the repercussions of last weekend’s win for the far-right Alternative für Deutschland party in the former communist state of Saxony-Anhalt, German commentators expressed a sense of doom, panic and helplessness in the political establishment.With nearly 44% of the vote, the AfD fell three seats short of an absolute majority. Its media savvy chief candidate, Ulrich Siegmund, is racing to find enough support from the other parties to prop up what would be the first rightwing extremist state government since the Nazi period.AfD co-leaders Alice Weidel (right) and Tino Chrupalla (left) with Saxony-Anhalt lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund. Photograph: Ebrahim Noroozi/APIt is still anyone’s guess whether he will succeed, leaving a corrosive uncertainty at the heart of Europe’s top economic power. Hanging in the balance is the fate of Friedrich Merz’s centre-right government, once called “democracy’s last shot” to prevent an extremist takeover in Germany.The result in Saxony-Anhalt has put the conservative chancellor on the ropes, with further punishment for his Christian Democratic Union party (CDU) expected in two more state polls later this month.“This is the worst defeat for the CDU in years – decades – and something has changed, not just in Saxony-Anhalt but in all of Germany,” he said on Monday.Whether or not he survives politically until the next general election, due in 2029, will have dramatic repercussions for Germany and its European allies trying to beat back anti-democratic forces.

articles.title: ‘Absurd, hardline calls’: questions over Sweden’s post-Brexit migration policy
articles.excerpt: He arrived with nothing other than the clothes he wore that morning. Hours later he was banged up in a detention centre close to a Stockholm airport to await deportation.Charles, a former business director from Cambridge, who did not want his full name published, moved to Sweden in 2017 to be with his Swedish wife, Lily, and applied to remain after Brexit, before the deadline of December 2021.But the migration agency rejected his application, and he and his wife have been fighting with the Swedish authorities ever since.In a message passed on by Lily, he said he was the only Briton in the detention centre, where he described being hemmed in by three lines of fences separated by a “no man’s land”.“I arrived here with nothing apart from the clothes I had on,” Charles said. “We were told the meeting … with the border police was to discuss my case. They then said they thought I would abscond, which is why they were going to detain me.”Lily, a lawyer, questioned whether Sweden, considered a global leader in human rights and progressive politics, was now like Afghanistan. “They have hunted us for five years,” she said.Charles could be deported in the next week unless his latest legal challenge delivers a reprieve.He joins a list of 2,490 Britons – of an estimated 14,000 in Sweden – deported from the country between 2020 and 2025, as questions are mounting as to why Sweden appears to have taken such a hardline approach to the Brexit withdrawal agreement (WA) over migration.In total, Sweden is responsible for 33% of all British nationals deported from the EU between 2021 and 2025, compared with France, which accounted for 6% of all British deportees, Spain at 3% and Germany at 2%.

articles.title: Houthis claim attack on Saudi base as fighting flares with Yemeni forces

articles.summary: 胡塞武装战士周日表示，他们使用无人机和导弹袭击了沙特阿拉伯南部的一处军事基地，与此同时，与也门政府军重新爆发的战斗导致越来越多的平民逃离。胡塞武装军事发言人叶海亚·萨里在X上写道，对南部沙鲁拉基地的袭击针对的是「正在指挥对我国和人民侵略的武器库及指挥控制中心」。此次行动的具体日期未予说明。

articles.title: Saudi Arabia shuts down key oil pipeline, blaming drones from Iraq
articles.excerpt: Saudi Arabia has shut down a critical oil pipeline, accusing militants in Iraq of launching drone attacks on the export route being used to bypass the lockdown of the strait of Hormuz.The world’s largest ⁠crude oil exporter has increased its use of the 745-mile (1,200km) pipeline running across the Arabian peninsula, which links Abqaiq, near the Gulf, to the port of Yanbu, on the Red Sea, since the US-Israeli war against Iran began.The Saudi foreign ministry condemned “the targeting of the East-West pipeline in the Riyadh and Medina regions by several drones coming from Iraq, which caused human injuries and damage”.An energy ministry official told the SPA news agency earlier that the pipeline was “stopped as a precaution”.Baghdad is under mounting pressure to prevent militant groups, including those backed by Saudi Arabia’s regional rival Iran, from launching attacks on Gulf countries from Iraqi soil.The US president, Donald Trump, said he believed Tehran was responsible for the aerial attack. “I ‌think they ‌are, probably they are,” Trump told reporters in ‌Dublin during a visit to Ireland.On Saturday, Iraq’s government confirmed the attacks were launched from its territory and ordered an investigation. It condemned “the attacks targeting our brethren in the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia”, and the office of the Iraqi prime minister, Ali al-Zaidi, said the commander in charge of the southern province of Maysan had been dismissed.Satellite images from Copernicus Sentinel Data taken on Thursday showed black smoke billowing near Medina, along the general route of the East-West pipeline.Black smoke over an area of the East-West pipeline south of Medina.

articles.title: IDF soldier filmed shooting Palestinian in leg amid West Bank settler standoff
articles.excerpt: An Israeli soldier has shot a Palestinian man, wounding him in the leg, as settlers confronted villagers by grazing livestock on Palestinian-owned land in the town of Faqqua in the occupied West Bank.Witnesses said a group of settlers had entered the area with their livestock, prompting residents to try to stop them. Israeli forces then intervened and, according to men at the scene, opened fire at residents. One of them shot Qassem Hussam, a Palestinian man in his mid-30s, wounding him in the leg.Israeli forces shoot Palestinian man in the leg in West Bank village – videoReached by the Guardian, the IDF confirmed it had received a report of the incident and that the person who fired was one of its soldiers.“Earlier today [Saturday], a report was received regarding friction between Israeli civilians and Palestinians near the area of Faqqua,” the IDF said. “An IDF force that was at the scene fired into the air and toward a Palestinian.”Mohammed al-Sheikh, 34, who was standing next to Hussam, told the Guardian the confrontation began when villagers encountered Israeli settlers grazing livestock on Palestinian-owned land.“Then the Israeli soldiers came,” al-Sheikh said. “They started shooting. One soldier shot Hussam and he fell to the ground. We immediately went to help him and move him away. We couldn’t get an ambulance to the area, so we took him to hospital in a private car.”Hussam was taken to hospital in a light-to-moderate condition, according to the Palestine Red Crescent.The Israeli military said the incident was being reviewed by commanders and that its findings would be forwarded to the relevant authorities for examination.

articles.title: Iran’s Houthi allies capture strategic island on vital oil shipping route
articles.excerpt: Yemen’s rampant Houthi forces have captured the strategic island of Perim in the Bab al-Mandab strait, expanding their control of the narrow waterway, one of the ​world’s vital shipping routes.The Iran-aligned Houthis took control of the volcanic island after forces allied to the UN-backed, Aden-based government left in the latest of a dramatic series of reverses along Yemen’s west coast in recent days, including the loss of the port city of Mocha on Thursday.Saudi Arabia, which supports and bankrolls the official Yemen government, mounted air raids on Houthi positions in Mocha on Friday.The Bab al-Mandab strait links Asia to Europe via the Red Sea and Suez canal. Perim island, also known as Mayun, divides the waterway in two, close to its narrowest point. The United Arab Emirates, a former Saudi ally in the anti-Houthi coalition, had been building an airbase on the island before ending its active involvement in the conflict in January.Houthi advance mapSaudi Arabia has increasingly relied on the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandab to export its crude since Iran has been targeting vessels in the strait of Hormuz. About 12% of the world’s goods are typically shipped through the strait.Saudi Arabia has now said it has shut down a crucial pipeline a day after it was attacked by drones, and Yemen’s Iranian-backed Houthi rebels captured Perim.It said it had shut its East-West pipeline as “a precautionary measure”, blaming the attack on several drones that came from Iraq.

articles.title: Nearly 50,000 Yemeni civilians flee as Houthis advance along Red Sea coast
articles.excerpt: Nearly 50,000 people have fled a sudden advance by Houthi forces in western Yemen, with entire villages emptied and families trapped near frontline fighting with depleting food supplies, according to aid workers.Civilians in the Middle East’s poorest country have found themselves victims of a global struggle for control over one of the most important shipping routes in the world, which threatens to turn Yemen’s on-off conflict into a forever war.In a lightning advance this week, the Iran-backed Houthi militants have seized a string of towns along the Red Sea coast from forces aligned with the US- and Saudi-backed Yemeni government. Hundreds of people are reported to have been killed. Many fear a return to the full-scale civil war that killed 150,000 and brought many others to the brink of famine.Map of Yemen marking recent Houthi movementsThe UN International Organization for Migration (IOM) said on Friday that 46,000 people had been displaced across the governates of Taiz and Hodeidah, where steep verdant mountain ridges give way to arid coastal plains. For many families, this was their second or even third time they had been forced out of their homes.A significant number of people were observed to be leaving the city with their belongings. Fighting has cut key roads, while phone lines are down in some areas. “The scale of displacement is increasing rapidly,” said Joe Lowry, IOM’s Middle East and north Africa spokesperson in Cairo.A heavily laden vehicle arrives in Sana’a as people flee frontline fighting. Photograph: Yahya Arhab/EPAThe most urgent needs were emergency shelters, cash assistance, food, drinking water, household items, healthcare and protection services.

articles.title: 'People are still afraid of those three letters': Fighting the stigma of HIV
articles.excerpt: Retired rugby star Gareth Thomas, who is HIV positive, came to Rio de Janeiro's famed Ipanema Beach to participate in a campaign called "Tackle HIV." Ian Cheibub for NPR hide caption toggle caption Ian Cheibub for NPR RIO DE JANEIRO -- "People are still afraid of those three letters," says Gareth Thomas, a former Welsh rugby star. He's talking about HIV. Thomas became a global champion for people living with HIV when he announced that he was HIV positive in 2019. Since then, he has been a strong advocate for sharing knowledge about the virus –- and what it's like to live with it. This summer, he came to Rio de Janeiro to participate in the International AIDS Conference and to spread his message as part of the Tackle HIV campaign. "I thought I was gonna die" That message resonates with another advocate: Welton Gabriel, a 36-year-old event organizer from Sao Paolo. Sitting in a bar overlooking the world-famous Ipanema beach, Welton Gabriel recalled the night 12 years earlier when he learned he had tested positive for HIV. When Welton Gabriel told close friends that he was HIV positive, many cut contact. "They did not want to talk with me," recalls Gabriel, who is now an activist combating the stigma of HIV. He was photographed during the AIDS Conference in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, this summer. Ian Cheibub for NPR hide caption toggle caption Ian Cheibub for NPR "I thought I was gonna die," he remembers. For a while, his life did hang in the balance. Gabriel had contracted a treatment-resistant strain of HIV — he believes that the sexual partner who infected him had been taking medication but decided to stop, allowing the virus to mutate. It took seven months before doctors were able to get the infection under control. "The amount of virus in my body was really high," he says. "I was initially started on a medicine that gave me a lot of problems with my liver, and my eyes became yellow.

articles.title: 'BRICS' forum brings together emerging economies, aimed at countering western dominance
articles.excerpt: India hosts the 18th BRICS summit in New Delhi this weekend. BRICS is a grouping of major emerging markets and developing countries. Transcript SCOTT SIMON, HOST: A summit meeting is taking place in New Delhi that includes countries - Iran and several Gulf nations - who are now at war. It's a meeting of a group called BRICS, and it represents about half of the population of the world. We're joined now from New Delhi by NPR's international correspondent Diaa Hadid. Diaa, thanks very much for being with us.DIAA HADID, BYLINE: Thank you, Scott.SIMON: What's the summit about?HADID: Well, BRICS is effectively a forum for emerging economies. It's aimed at countering long-standing Western dominance, and there's leaders from more than a dozen countries who've turned up. And, Scott, it's quite the gathering. China's president, Xi Jinping, and Russia's president, Vladimir Putin, are here. But for now, the attention is on those involved in the latest Mideast war, because the Iranian president is here, and Iran has been striking Gulf countries that are also at the summit - the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain and Saudi Arabia. And that's because Iran accuses them of backing the United States.And just to set the scene a bit, the summit today comes just a day after Iranian-backed fighters in Yemen - they're known as the Houthis - appeared to consolidate control over another shipping route called Bab el-Mandeb. That route was emerging as an alternative for some Gulf oil exports through the Strait of Hormuz. You might recall that strait has been largely blocked since the Mideast war began in February.SIMON: Dramatic ingredients for a meeting. How has it played out so far?HADID: So far, the Iranian president, Masoud Pezeshkian, has told audiences here that Iran and Oman have agreed on a joint route through the Strait of Hormuz, and they'll sign a deal on Monday.

articles.title: Saudi Arabia forced to shut down crucial Red Sea pipeline after attacks
articles.excerpt: The Iran-backed Houthi militia captured a strategic Red Sea port city this week. NPR's Scott Simon talks to April Longley Alley of the Washington Institute. Transcript SCOTT SIMON, HOST: Saudi Arabia, the world's largest exporter of oil, says that it has shut down a crucial pipeline after it was attacked by drones. The kingdom was relying on the east-west pipeline to export oil via the Red Sea, bypassing the Strait of Hormuz. But now Saudi Arabia is also facing a growing threat on the Red Sea after Iran-backed Houthi rebels made a series of military gains this week. We're joined now by April Longley Alley, a senior fellow at The Washington Institute and an expert on Yemen. Thanks so much for being with us.APRIL LONGLEY ALLEY: Thank you for having me.SIMON: What do we know about the Houthi advances in Yemen over the past few days?ALLEY: The most important development is that the Houthis have broken front lines in Yemen. And on Thursday, they captured the strategic port city of Mokha, on the Red Sea coast. And then they quickly punched south. And by Friday, they had taken the entire Red Sea coastline, down to the strategic Bab el-Mandeb choke point. And remember, the Houthis are Iranian-backed. They're a militant group, and they control most of North Yemen.But this did not come out of nowhere. Yemen's war has been heating up, and there's been a series of tit-for-tat escalations between the Houthis on one hand and Saudi Arabia and the Saudi-backed Yemeni government on the other. But what we saw this week and last week was a sharp escalation in violence, you know, at a time when the region's in flux.SIMON: What will the impact be? As we mentioned, Saudi Arabia has been forced to shut down this key pipeline. What will the impact be on Saudi Arabia and the global economy if it can't get oil through the Red Sea?ALLEY: It is really huge. I mean, there are just limits to redundancy when it comes to the ability of Aramco to export oil.

articles.title: The secret quest to preserve Palestinian writer Raja Shehadeh's diaries
articles.excerpt: Raja Shehadeh looks at folders from his archive in 2026. Yazeed Abu Khdeir hide caption toggle caption Yazeed Abu Khdeir The world's leading Palestinian writer, Raja Shehadeh, has been on a mission to save his most personal work: his diaries. The award-winning author of more than 20 books has been documenting decades of Palestinian life, starting in 1967 at the very beginning of Israel's occupation of the West Bank when he was a teenager. Raja Shehadeh's first diary entry from May 11, 1967. Raja Shehadeh hide caption toggle caption Raja Shehadeh His diaries capture a unique voice and front row view of history: his meetings with world leaders, his work as a human rights lawyer, and his role as legal advisor to the Palestinians during peace talks with Israel. Shehadeh, now 75, feared his diaries and archives — kept in his garage in the West Bank city of Ramallah — were at risk of destruction from Israeli military operations. (The Israeli foreign ministry did not respond to requests for comment about Shehadeh's fears.) Yazeed Abu Khdeir (left) and Mahmoud Muna work to digitize papers, as Raja Shehadeh (standing) looks on. Hannah Harper hide caption toggle caption Hannah Harper So he took part in a two-year, discreet effort to spirit them to Scotland, where he has spent many summers. The archives are now at the University of Edinburgh, and the University of Exeter in England has published thousands of pages online. Shehadeh spoke with NPR's Daniel Estrin about his decades of diary writing, and the secret effort to preserve his archives. The interview text below has been edited for length and clarity. How keeping a diary consistently for so long impacted who he is as a writer It's been a daily effort...in order to understand better what is happening around me, in order to record and document what is happening. I started when I was...fifteen years old, just before the occupation.

articles.title: BRICS leaders meet in India as wars and US tensions test the bloc
articles.excerpt: Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, center right, arrives for the BRICS summit in New Delhi, India, Friday, Sept. 11, 2026. (Indian Foreign Ministry via AP) Indian Foreign Ministry via AP/Indian Foreign Ministry hide caption toggle caption Indian Foreign Ministry via AP/Indian Foreign Ministry Leaders of the BRICS nations are meeting in New Delhi on Saturday for a summit focused on trade, investment and global conflicts, as the bloc seeks a bigger role in shaping the global agenda for emerging and developing countries. Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi is hosting Russian President Vladimir Putin, Chinese President Xi Jinping, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and counterparts from the other eight BRICS members. The summit comes as wars in Ukraine and the Middle East, along with rising U.S.-China tensions, test the bloc's ability to find common ground among countries with competing geopolitical interests. Thousands of police and paramilitary personnel were deployed around the summit venue and other parts of New Delhi, with traffic restrictions and diversions in place. BRICS was founded in 2006 by Brazil, Russia, India and China, with South Africa joining in 2010. It has since expanded to 11 members, representing about half the world's population and a significant share of global economic output. The group has increasingly called for greater representation for developing countries in global institutions. The leaders are expected to discuss economic cooperation, energy, food security, technology, supply chains and reforms to global institutions. Reducing reliance on the U.S. dollar will also be a priority, with members promoting greater use of their own currencies in trade and payments, as well as pushing for alternatives to Western-dominated financial institutions.
