articles.title: AI, Robotics and the Coming Economic, Military, and Political Revolutions
articles.excerpt: Features | Economy | East Asia In the context of ongoing transformations to the economy, society, and military, China’s current strategy is particularly alarming, and potentially transformational. A humanoid service robot as a cashier in an automated convenience store selling drinks in Shanghai, China, Nov. 28, 2025. Credit: Shutterstock As China’s President Xi Jinping prepares to travel to Washington, D.C. on September 24, his approach will reflect not only the specific items on his agenda, but also broader geopolitical transformations currently underway. These revolutions-in-progress create both enormous opportunities for China and hazards for it, and the international community, to navigate. Reinforcing advances currently underway in “big data,” artificial intelligence (AI), autonomous systems, and robotics are rapidly transforming both economic and military dynamics, with radical implications for political systems and the global balance of power. Latin America and the rest of the developing world will be a battleground, a beneficiary, and a victim in that enormous and chaotic change. Although the future cannot be predicted with certainty, one reasonable outcome of the current confluence of trends is a world that is far more violent, less democratic, and more dominated by China. That future could emerge more rapidly than most traditional analysts expect. Here’s how such traumatic and revolutionary change could occur, and what it could mean for the United States, Latin America, and the world. The Coming AI-Robotics Revolution Within the next decade, developments arising out of the synergy between artificial intelligence and robotics will likely present non-human alternatives to a wide variety of both white-collar and blue-collar, skilled and unskilled labor, transforming a far broader range of work, far more rapidly than occurred in last century’s industrial revolution.

articles.title: SCO Summit Produces Surprising Winners
articles.excerpt: The Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) summit in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan August 31-September 1 marked a quarter century since the organization’s founding. Its anniversary motto, “Together for Sustainable Peace, Development and Prosperity,” hinted at ambitions considerably grander than the institution’s record. The SCO now encompasses ten member states, including China, India, Russia, Iran, Pakistan, and four Central Asian republics – Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, and Uzbekistan – representing nearly half of humanity and a substantial share of global economic activity. Yet headlines emerging from Bishkek often highlighted the organization’s internal dynamics and differing national priorities. Unlike last year’s summit, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi did not hold a formal bilateral meeting, although their brief interaction during the summit quickly became a meme template among Indian netizens. Modi and Pakistan’s Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif traded predictable barbs. Most stunningly, Modi directly urged Russian President Vladimir Putin to end the war in Ukraine “for humanity’s sake.” This comes shortly after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy revealed that China delivered an ultimatum to Russia not to use nuclear weapons in Ukraine, something China has not denied. This focus on discord is not merely dramatic headline chasing; it reflects a genuine and consistently noted problem with the SCO. The organization brings together several geopolitical rivals. It is therefore difficult to imagine the institution ever evolving into a mirror of NATO. The SCO lacks the degree of institutionalization necessary to impose coherent policy on its members, while its principal powers lack sufficient leverage over one another to establish a common strategic direction. But these features should not lead observers to dismiss the organization’s practical value for its members, especially the smaller ones.

articles.title: What Role Does Denuclearization Have in North Korea-US Dialogue Today?
articles.excerpt: With his surprise decision to scale back the recent Ulchi Freedom Shield military exercise on the Korean Peninsula, U.S. President Donald Trump clearly signaled his intent to rekindle dialogue with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un. However, rather than receiving praise for the goodwill measure, the effort drew rebuke from the North Korean government, which reiterated its position that it has no interest in renewing engagement as long as the United States holds onto denuclearization as a policy objective. This exchange has renewed debates over long-standing denuclearization policies, particularly as Trump continues his overtures toward the Kim regime in hopes of a possible meeting on the sidelines of the APEC summit in November. Some have argued it is time to abandon denuclearization as a policy goal and shift to arms control, while others contend that such a concession would undermine the global nonproliferation regime and place further stress on allied relationships. Rather than a binary “should they, shouldn’t they” approach, the issue requires a more nuanced examination of the constraints and interests at play. For example, what does the Kim regime mean when it demands that foreign governments drop denuclearization as a precondition for talks? What does the Trump administration hope to achieve by renewing engagement? Further, would dropping denuclearization even be politically sustainable for this administration or other governments? It’s useful to break down the denuclearization debate, examining the knowns and unknowns for the two sides. Trump’s Overtures and North Korea’s Response On August 16, Trump announced the shortening of the annual South Korea-U.S. Ulchi Freedom Shield joint military exercise, reiterating his usual claim that the exercises are costly and adding that they “send a signal that is totally inappropriate and hostile” to North Korea. He claimed that the Kim regime has been “unthreatening and respectful” during his presidency.

articles.title: Can India Exploit China’s ‘Malacca Dilemma’?
articles.excerpt: India faces one of the most challenging security environments in the world, confronting not one but two adversarial neighbors: Pakistan and China. While New Delhi retains the conventional military upper hand over Islamabad, in Beijing it confronts a militarily and economically superior power that has repeatedly used force to alter the status quo along their disputed border. Since the 1962 border war, India and China have faced a series of military confrontations, including the 2017 Doklam standoff and the deadly Galwan Valley clashes in 2020. More recently, Beijing reportedly provided Islamabad with critical intelligence support during the 2025 India-Pakistan conflict, raising the likelihood that any future Indo-Pak crisis will unfold against the backdrop of Chinese support for Islamabad. Given this geopolitical reality, India must prepare to deter and, if needed, confront future Chinese aggression. Although formidable, India’s military remains conventionally weaker than China’s. At $92 billion, New Delhi’s defense spending is just over a quarter of Beijing’s. Despite India’s efforts to procure advanced Western fighter jets and develop its own indigenous capabilities, China still enjoys a 3:1 advantage in airpower, and its naval modernization far outpaces India’s own efforts. Fortunately for India, it does not need to match China’s military capabilities one-to-one to establish credible deterrence. The ongoing conflict in the Gulf presents yet another lesson in how it can use asymmetric warfare to its advantage. Over the past six months, Iran has demonstrated its ability to threaten commercial shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, disrupting global energy markets and imposing disproportionate costs on conventionally superior military powers. China, too, has a major maritime vulnerability.

articles.title: The Mecca Pact: A New Treaty Organization, Just Like the Old One
articles.excerpt: Much has been made of the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement (MJDA) – a collective security agreement signed by Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, and Turkiye in early August – in news and analysis recently. Some have likened this to the Russia-dominated Collective Security Treaty Organization (CSTO). Others have called this a signal of the end of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) and the birth of a new regional order. Though, perhaps reports of NATO’s death are greatly exaggerated. And with the benefit of a longer historical lens, we can see how prognostications that MJDA will remake the region’s security are fairly off the mark. More than anything, MJDA resembles the failed and somewhat forgotten Central Treaty Organization (CENTO) of the Cold War. And, we can expect that, like CENTO, the member states themselves, and those around them, will continue their defense and security planning much as they have before. MJDA is unlikely to solve the problems it purports to confront and will accomplish little more than the Cold War’s CENTO. For a closer modern analogue, perhaps look to the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) structure, a forum for warm promises and suppressed disgruntlement. But for a moment, let’s turn back the clock. CENTO was launched as the Baghdad Pact in 1955, a defensive agreement between Iran, Iraq, Pakistan, Turkiye (then spelled Turkey), and the United Kingdom, with the United States initially serving as an observer. This was a reaction to the failing World War II global alliance system and the emergence of new security challenges – specifically, the split between capitalism and communism. Regionally, secular powers in and around the Middle East feared that a reemergent Soviet Union would follow the path of tsarist Russia. They anticipated that a desire for warm-water ports and hydrocarbons (mainly oil at the time) would drive Moscow’s perceived designs on the Mediterranean Sea, the Persian Gulf, and even the Indian Ocean.

articles.title: Learning Chinese Sign Language
articles.excerpt: Learning Chinese Sign Language is a bewildering experience. To begin with, Chinese Sign Language (CSL) is in itself best understood as an umbrella term rather than a well-defined language. You have Signed Chinese, shoushi hanyu, which is one-to-one transcriptions of the written standard Chinese into signs, replete with interpuncation such as signed question marks. Then there is Natural Sign Language, ziran shouyu, the language that is actually spoken between native deaf signers in China. It has syntax and grammar markedly different from Chinese, makes extensive use of abbreviations and, like all natural sign languages, incorporates facial expressions. Besides these, there are yet other types of CSL described in the academic literature, such as Literary Sign Language (wenfa shouyu) and Society Sign Language (shehui shouyu). All the more confusing is how these terms often seem to overlap or even are used interchangeably. Since 2018, the government has been actively promoting a type of sign language titled Guojia Tongyong Shouyu, sometimes translated into English as Chinese General Sign Language (CGSL). According to the Chinese Ministry of Education, CGSL can be seen as the sign language equivalent to Standard Mandarin. Having moved away from a standard based on spoken or written Chinese, CGSL incorporates elements from the natural sign languages and thus appears to be less alien to native deaf speakers. While this standardized variety has been described by some Chinese academics as a “natural sign language,” it is, however, uncertain if it is viewed as such by deaf Chinese themselves. For the prospective learner, there is a surprisingly user-friendly app based on the official CGSL lexicon. There are daily quizzes, signed demonstrations of the words, targeted tests, themed glossaries, and other useful tools for learning. Unfortunately, all of this does not compensate for the staggering lack of lexemes in the dictionary.

articles.title: Bangladesh and the Perils of Pax Silica
articles.excerpt: The Pulse | Diplomacy | South Asia It could end up exchanging strategic flexibility for an upgraded version of the subcontracting economy it is trying to escape. U.S. Special Envoy for South and Central Asia Sergio Gor with Bangladesh’s Prime Minister Tarique Rahman at a meeting in Dhaka, Bangladesh, August 1, 2026. Credit: X/Bangladesh Nationalist Party-BNP On August 1, U.S. Special Envoy for South and Central Asia Sergio Gor presented a consequential proposition to Bangladesh’s Prime Minister Tarique Rahman to join Pax Silica. “The country has significant potential to become a partner in the global economic security alliance focused on artificial intelligence, semiconductors and critical mineral supply chains,” he said. On the same day, Dhaka announced that it would join the Shanghai-based World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization (WAICO), initially as an observer. Bangladesh therefore found itself courted by two emerging technology orders in a single news cycle. The invitation deserves neither reflexive rejection nor diplomatic applause. It demands a national strategy. What, then, should Bangladesh do? Pax Silica was launched in Washington in December 2025 with seven declaration signatories to “build a secure, prosperous, and innovation-driven silicon supply chain — from critical minerals and energy inputs to advanced manufacturing, semiconductors, AI infrastructure and logistics.” By mid-August 2026, 25 countries, including the U.S., U.K., Japan, Singapore and India, had signed on. Pax Silica is not simply about chips. Its ambition covers the full artificial intelligence stack: minerals, refining, electricity, data infrastructure, semiconductor design and production, logistics, advanced manufacturing, models, and digital platforms. The State Department describes the goal as reducing coercive dependencies and creating trusted supply chains. The geopolitical interest is equally clear.

articles.title: Namal Rajapaksa’s Arrest and Sri Lanka’s Politics of Mutual Protection
articles.excerpt: Sri Lankan investigators arrested Namal Rajapaksa on September 4 over allegations that he received 100 million Sri Lankan rupees (about $800,000 per 2014-15 exchange rates) in bribes linked to an aircraft procurement deal involving SriLankan Airlines in 2012-13. The arrest shows that investigators have moved beyond airline officials and business intermediaries to a member of Sri Lanka’s most powerful political family. The reaction to the arrest was interesting. The United National Party (UNP), which led the 2015-19 Yahapalanaya (good governance) government under which several investigations against Rajapaksa began, joined the Rajapaksa family-led Sri Lanka Podujana Peramuna (SLPP) in condemning his arrest. Their response also demonstrates why a political party from outside the UNP-SLPP establishment needed to be in power to pursue investigations against powerful politicians. Most of the political opposition and their allies in the media and religious establishments have come out in support of the Rajapaksas, and enormous resources are being spent to discredit the arrest of Namal. Thus, the question is not merely whether Namal will be convicted, but whether the National People’s Power (NPP) anti-corruption campaign can survive contact with the same political pressures that neutered every previous attempt to hold Sri Lanka’s elites to account. A Money Trail Left Unfinished In 2020, Airbus agreed to pay nearly $4 billion to settle international bribery investigations. As part of the investigations, foreign officials traced suspicious payments linked to SriLankan Airlines’ aircraft purchases, and a British court made details of the transactions public. In response, the Gotabaya Rajapaksa government arrested former SriLankan Airlines CEO Kapila Chandrasena and his wife. But the investigation went no further; the two were released on bail, and no action was taken to determine whether Chandrasena and others worked with politicians.

articles.title: Asia’s Economic Integration: A Roadmap for Peacebuilding in the Middle East
articles.excerpt: The Debate Economic cooperation in the Asia-Pacific has been the key driver of peace since 1952. Credit: Facebook/Dato’ Seri Utama Haji Mohamad Bin Haji Hasan When the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, ASEAN, was formed in 1967, the five founding states intended to produce a front against the spread of communism. The venture has since grown to include a total of 11 countries, producing a remarkable set of unforeseen consequences, from becoming the fifth-largest economy in the world to reinforcing peace across a swath of diverse and developing countries. Instead of pursuing Cold War initiatives, the bloc has become increasingly integrated, tied together through manufacturing supply chains, trade infrastructure, and shared financial institutions like the Chiang Mai Initiative. ASEAN now produces over $4 trillion in GDP and has a population of 678 million people. The collaboration’s biggest success, however, has not simply been increased commerce. With economic integration comes regional stabilization and peace, a consequence further fostered by the signing of the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP) in 2020, which includes Australia, China, Japan, New Zealand, and South Korea. Economic cooperation in the Asia-Pacific has been the key driver of peace in the region ever since 1952 with the Treaty of San Francisco, and it serves today as a key example of how market mechanics can drive peacebuilding. In fact, it was ASEAN that eroded tensions from the Konfrontasi war in the early 1960s, and has solidified the climate of peace between the Southeast Asian members ever since. Economists and politicians have often considered the question of whether trade contributes to peaceful relations between states. The affirmative answer is not novel; however, in the case of ASEAN and the Asia-Pacific, the specifics begin to clarify the theory.

articles.title: After the Bangsamoro Poll, Can Politics Maintain the Peace?
articles.excerpt: On September 14, more than 2.3 million registered voters in the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) in the southern Philippines will go to the polls for the first regular parliamentary election. The immediate priority is that the elections should be peaceful, orderly, and credible, but beyond that there is another question that deserves attention: what will political competition look like in communities where political loyalties are changing, particularly in areas historically aligned with the Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF)? The answer could have important consequences for the peace process. Election-related violence is not new to the Bangsamoro. It long predates the peace agreement with the MILF, and has often been associated with clan rivalries, private armed groups, and local political competition rooted in longstanding disputes. In many communities, elections can even appear relatively peaceful because political power is concentrated within a dominant family or network. The absence of violence, therefore, does not necessarily mean the absence of political contestation; sometimes, it simply reflects the absence of meaningful competition. As I have argued previously, the movement’s political environment has become increasingly fragmented. Former allies now find themselves competing through different political formations, including the United Bangsamoro Justice Party (UBJP) and the Bangsamoro Federalist Party (BFP). Some may remain aligned with UBJP, while others have moved toward BFP or other competing parties and candidates. This raises the question of whether former allies who once operated within a common political and organizational framework can compete against one another without reproducing the patterns of conflict that the peace process was designed to transform. There is a danger of interpreting every violent incident during the election period as evidence that the peace process is failing.

articles.title: From 9/11 to Pahalgam: India’s Evolving Strategy in the Global War on Terror
articles.excerpt: Some incidents in world history not only leave deep scars on the soul of a nation but alter the nation’s trajectory irreversibly. The terror attack of September 11, 2001 was one such incident. A perfectly normal morning turned into a horrific nightmare when 19 al-Qaida terrorists hijacked four passenger planes, two of which crashed into the Twin Towers in New York and one into the Pentagon building outside of Washington, D.C. The Twin Towers came crashing down and the result was a death count of almost 3,000. The resultant national outrage and anger led to the United States leading its most extensive military mission since the Vietnam War, chasing al-Qaida and its leader Osama bin Laden into Afghanistan. In a military campaign lasting almost 20 years, al-Qaida was largely neutralized and Osama bin Laden was eventually tracked and killed in Pakistan on May 2, 2011. The 9/11 attacks led to profound changes in the United States as well, especially in matters of internal security. There was a clear mandate that no matter what, there cannot be another 9/11 type of incident on the American mainland ever again. In the Indian context however, it took decades of terror attacks before India similarly said, “no more.” Thanks to a policy crafted by Pakistan in the early 1990s to “bleed India through a thousand cuts” with cross-border terrorism, India endured a large number of terror attacks and losses, especially in Kashmir. But then one terror incident shook India like never before. The terror attack in Pahalgam on April 22, 2025 killed 26 innocent civilians in a popular tourist spot in Kashmir. The attack was launched by terrorists belonging to The Resistance Force, an offshoot of the Pakistan-based Lashkar-e-Taiba (LeT). The anger and outrage in India were magnified many times over as the victims – all men – were specifically identified by their religion (Hindu, except for one Christian and one local Muslim who tried to intervene).

articles.title: From 9/11 to the Iran War, Pakistan-US Ties Remain Transactional
articles.excerpt: Twenty-five years ago, the September 11 attacks transformed Pakistan’s relationship with the United States. Almost overnight, Pakistan went from facing American sanctions and limited diplomatic attention to becoming a frontline partner in the U.S.-led war in Afghanistan. In its counterterrorism cooperation, Pakistan offered vital ground-and air-based logistical transit to Afghanistan as well as intelligence and military action. In return, the United States provided financial reimbursement and military assistance in the form of subsidized sale of military hardware and technology. The relationship became increasingly strained as the two sides accused each other of failing to deliver what had been promised. Yet the two sides remained close as long as Washington needed Pakistan for the war in Afghanistan. When the U.S. military withdrew from Afghanistan in August 2021, much of the urgency behind the relationship disappeared. Washington’s political attention declined, although counterterrorism, trade, health, and other forms of engagement continued at the institutional level. Twenty-five years after 9/11, Pakistan and the United States appear to have entered another period of warm relations. Pakistan has again presented itself as a useful partner through mediation between Washington and Tehran, alongside cryptocurrency deals, critical mineral investments, and counterterrorism cooperation. As Pakistan mediates in the Iran-U.S. war, given the difficulties of reaching a truce, there’s a constant fear of Pakistani leaders becoming the eventual fall guys. To avert that outcome, Islamabad has been investing significant time and resources to the success of the mediation efforts. The outcome has been far from assured. Some see this as another example of Pakistan over-promising and falling short of delivering. But there’s a bigger question behind recent events: Why does every revival of Pakistan-U.S. relations require another geopolitical crisis? The problem is that Pakistan-U.S.

articles.title: Tashiev and the Letter of 75: Charges Reclassified, Sentences Lessened, Confusion Reigns
articles.excerpt: When the trial of the former head of Kyrgyzstan’s State Committee for National Security, Kamchybek Tashiev, ended in July the judge delivered what appeared to be a damning verdict followed by an absurdist reprieve. Tashiev – alongside former Speaker of the Zhogorku Kenesh Nurlanbek Turgunbek uulu, former Member of Parliament Kurmankul Zulushev, and five others – was found guilty of a coup attempt under Article 326 (“Violent seizure or retention of power, as well as an attempt to violently change the constitutional order”) of the Kyrgyz criminal code and acquitted of abuse of office charges. Tashiev and the rest were sentenced to four years in prison – the prosecutors had sought nine. The judge immediately replaced the prison terms with three years of supervised probation. Tashiev, technically convicted of a coup attempt, served not a single day in detention. Both Tashiev’s lawyers and the prosecutors filed appeals, the former seeking complete acquittal and the latter harsher sentencing. In early September, the Bishkek City Court heard the appeal. Like most of the first trial, the proceedings were held behind closed doors, so what happened next doesn’t have a clear explanation. The court apparently reclassified the charges from a coup attempt under Article 326 to “obstruction of the exercise of electoral rights,” Article 195. According to various lawyers representing the defendants, all eight were sentenced to four year prison terms, converted immediately to two years of probation. Zhoomart Ashirbaev, the lawyer for Zulushev, told RFE/RL’s Kyrgyz Service, Azattyk, that they intended to file a cassation appeal with the Supreme Court. “The court’s reclassification of the charge from a serious crime to Article 195 demonstrates that the investigation brought an unfounded and unproven charge. I spoke with Kurmankul Zulushev immediately after the verdict was announced.

articles.title: What the AfD’s Rise in Germany Means for China-EU Relations
articles.excerpt: The September 6 state election in Saxony-Anhalt, Germany, resulted in a decisive victory for Alternative for Germany (AfD), which secured nearly 44 percent of the vote. It marked a stunning rise for the party, which is widely considered to belong to the far-right of the political spectrum. While the AfD’s performance is fundamentally a domestic political development driven by local grievances, energy costs, and other factors, this outcome offers an important, often overlooked perspective on the economic policy dialogue between the EU and China. The rapid ascent of Chinese firms in key sectors like automotive and chemicals has accelerated pressure on legacy European manufacturers. The subsequent corporate restructuring and job losses fuel public anxiety that political groups can leverage to gain ground. If this trend continues, short-term commercial gains for Chinese players could later give way to long-term operational hurdles, forcing them to navigate an EU defined by more political fragmentation and regulatory unpredictability. While not a silver bullet, adopting a more sustainable, localized engagement strategy in Europe offers Chinese enterprises a way to protect their market access while ensuring European host regions benefit as well. In the September 6 regional elections, the AfD won more than 40 percent of the votes, falling short of an outright majority but securing a win that signifies a crushing victory over incumbent Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s Christian Democratic Union, the popularity of which collapsed from above 37 percent in 2021 to below 18 percent. On the surface, a regional election in eastern Germany may seem distant from the EU’s foreign trade policy. A closer look, however, suggests otherwise. The AfD’s success draws attention to an often overlooked dimension in the ongoing China-EU economic debate: the impact on European political dynamics.

articles.title: Can Southeast Asia Benefit From the China-US AI Race?
articles.excerpt: Southeast Asia’s familiar predicament – being asked to choose between Washington and Beijing – is acquiring an artificial intelligence dimension. In August, Reuters reported that a draft U.S. State Department letter warned partners against combining participation in Pax Silica, the U.S.-led technology initiative, with competing arrangements. The letter didn’t include specific names, but the obvious inference was that Washington was trying to discourage participation in China’s World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization (WAICO). The draft was undated, and Reuters could not establish if it would be sent or whether it would change. Even so, its political ambition was clear: Washington wanted cooperation on AI to carry a stronger expectation of alignment. For Southeast Asian governments, the danger extends beyond an uncomfortable diplomatic decision. Technology agreements made today can shape which choices remain affordable tomorrow. If a country’s businesses and public services become heavily dependent on one foreign supplier, resisting that supplier’s government may become more costly even without a formal demand to take sides. The region therefore needs to negotiate development benefits and political room for maneuver together, while competing powers still have reasons to court Southeast Asia. Separate U.S. and Chinese initiatives are drawing countries into different bargains. Pax Silica, launched in December 2025, brings together countries seeking closer cooperation across technology supply chains, from critical minerals to AI systems. Its appeal lies in the prospect of investment, industrial partnerships, and advanced American technology. WAICO began with 29 countries signing its founding agreement in Shanghai on July 16. By August 12, Foreign Minister Wang Yi reported 38 founding members.

articles.title: Another New Job for Saida Mirziyoyeva: Manager of the Tashkent International Financial Center
articles.excerpt: Saida Mirziyoyeva has another new job. By presidential decree – that is, by order of her own father, President Shavkat Mirziyoyev, whose administration she heads – Mirziyoyeva has been appointed manager of the Tashkent International Financial Center (TIFC). The TIFC was proposed in a March 2026 presidential decree as part of an effort to bring in long-term foreign direct investment. The financial center aims to attract investors in a range of industries from banking, investment, and insurance services to digital assets, Islamic finance, and green tech, in addition to professional services like auditing, legal counsel, and fintech. Signed into law in July, the TIFC will operate under a special legal regime, based on English law, with a unique regulatory framework and an independent commercial court. With this arrangement, Uzbekistan seeks to address long-standing concerns foreign investors have had by carving out a legal space that isn’t governed strictly by Uzbek law. In pursuit of attracting foreign investors, those engaged in the TIFC will reportedly be able to hire foreigners without obtaining the usually required work permits and take advantage of special entry visa options. They will be allowed use foreign currency or cryptocurrency for payments and other monetary obligations and will benefit from tax and customs breaks until 2076. In announcing the signing of the law in July by Mirziyoyev, Mirziyoyeva said on social media, “This is one of the most important pieces of economic news of the year and the result of reforms that we pursued for almost ten years.” She went on to argue that the TIFC’s special structures “are the mechanisms to which global investors, banks, investment funds and international financial companies are accustomed.

articles.title: East Asia’s Quiet Race to Find the Universe’s Missing Mass
articles.excerpt: On September 1, 2026, physicists with the LUX-ZEPLIN (LZ) experiment, a ten-ton liquid xenon detector buried nearly a mile underground at the Sanford Underground Research Facility in South Dakota, announced they had recorded a single particle interaction that standard background processes struggle to explain. The event, drawn from 220 days of data collected between March 2023 and April 2024, sits at a statistical significance of about 2.6 sigma, far short of the 5-sigma threshold physicists require to claim a discovery, but it’s the strongest hint LZ has produced to date that a weakly interacting massive particle (WIMP) may have grazed its xenon target. It’s potentially a step forward in LZ’s main goal: to detect dark matter. LZ’s spokesperson, Professor Rick Gaitskell of Brown University, was careful to frame it as intriguing rather than conclusive. “With only one event, we don’t want to get ahead of ourselves,” he said. “We are not claiming to have seen dark matter. But we have seen something interesting that we want to share with the scientific community for their input.” His collaborators similarly stressed that unexpected backgrounds have fooled sensitive detectors before. Beyond the scientific question itself, it’s notable where the result was unveiled: not in the United States, but at the TeV Particle Astrophysics (TeVPA) 2026 conference in Japan. That is a small but telling sign of how central East Asia has become to the global effort to identify dark matter, the invisible substance thought to make up roughly 25 percent of all matter in the universe. Dark matter’s existence is inferred from galactic rotation and gravitational lensing, but it has never been directly observed. While LZ, Europe’s XENONnT, and Italy’s DarkSide-20k dominate headlines in the West, China, South Korea, and Japan run their own parallel programs, some of them world-leading in sensitivity, others aimed at settling decades-old controversies that Western experiments cannot resolve alone.

articles.title: What Kazakhstan’s New Unicameral Parliament Means for Its Foreign Policy
articles.excerpt: In early June, Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev signed enabling laws, putting into effect the new constitution passed via referendum in March 2026. Among the most significant changes was the abolishment of the bicameral parliament and its replacement with a new unicameral body, the Kurultai, whose 145 deputies were subsequently elected through party lists on August 23. While the domestic consequences of the changes to the legislature have been debated widely, the question of how they will affect Kazakhstan’s foreign policymaking remains underexamined. With the abolishment of the bicameral parliament – comprising an upper house, the Senate, and a lower house, the Mazhilis – the number of committees under the new legislature was reduced to eight, down from 13 (seven in the former Mazhilis and six in the Senate). Under Article 61 of the prior constitution, the dual-committee structure provided checks and balances within the legislative branch. The Mazhilis’s Committee on Foreign Affairs, Defense, and Security served as the primary chamber for drafting, amending, and holding preliminary readings for security and international agreements, while the Senate’s Committee on International Relations, Defense, and Security acted as a second layer of technical and diplomatic vetting. Treaties and defense pacts moved sequentially through both chambers and both committees. The Senate could approve, return for revisions, or reject a bill passed by the Mazhilis. Another structural change lies in how deputies are selected. In the previous bicameral parliament, the president could appoint a certain number of deputies, and often appointed seasoned diplomats such as former ambassadors, ex-ministers, and career officials. The most prominent example is the current president, Tokayev, who was twice appointed as Senate speaker.

articles.title: Why Is China Less Active in the 2026 Ebola Epidemic?
articles.excerpt: The Ebola epidemic spreading through the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) could become the largest Ebola outbreak on record if infections continue at their current pace. More than 6,700 people had been infected and more than 3,200 had died by September 2026. The outbreak is caused by Bundibugyo virus, a form of Ebola for which there is currently no licensed vaccine or approved treatment. The crisis is unfolding at a remarkable moment for global health. The United States is retreating from the global health system it once led. Beijing is the world’s second-largest economy and holds substantial interests in the DRC’s copper and cobalt industries. That matters not because Beijing has an obligation to replace Washington. Rather, the outbreak offers a test of whether, as the United States pulls back from global institutions, China will step forward. During the 2014-2016 West African Ebola outbreak, which caused approximately 11,325 deaths and more than 28,600 cases, China emerged as an unexpectedly prominent donor. By late 2014, Beijing had provided assistance valued at 750 million yuan, including laboratories, food aid, and health personnel. What was particularly striking, however, was the speed with which China’s aid arrived. Ebola was first detected in Guinea in March 2014, and by April, China had sent 4 million yuan worth of assistance. This was quickly followed by several firsts for Beijing, including the use of chartered flights to deliver humanitarian relief and the deployment of its first overseas infectious-disease field hospital. Western countries, on the other hand, were slower to react. It was not until the outbreak had expanded dramatically during the summer of 2014 that the United States, Britain, and other major donors mounted large-scale responses. By then, China had already been providing assistance for months. Although Western countries would ultimately contribute more money, the significance of China’s early response went beyond its dollar value.

articles.title: Why Have Indians Become a Regular Target of Hate in Singapore?
articles.excerpt: When Lee Kuan Yew took Singapore out of the Malaysian Federation on August 9, 1965, he made English the new nation’s primary language of government and education, rather than Chinese, despite the fact that 75 percent of the population was ethnic Chinese. Ensuring that other ethnic minorities did not feel alienated, he also gave Malay, Mandarin, and Tamil official status. After the race riots in 1964 that left 36 people dead, Lee dismantled the city’s deeply segregated colonial setup, where different ethnic groups lived in isolated enclaves, and introduced the Ethnic Integration Policy. This ensured that every building must have a mix of Chinese, Malay, and Indian residents that matches the country’s actual population. These steps played a major role in remaking Singapore from a colonial city-state into a developed nation. For more than 50 years, the edifice Lee erected remained intact. Given this background, the rise in racial attacks and derogatory slurs against the Indian community in the last few years look surprising, but the discontent against them has been simmering for a long time. The internet and social media have merely brought it to the fore. Suddenly, videos going viral about Indians littering beaches, misbehaving in public, or clashing with locals have circulated widely, sparking outrage and fueling stereotypes. For a country that prides itself on racial harmony, the intensity of this reaction is both striking and concerning. A number of recent incidents show that things have gone a bit too far. When reports came about nine Singaporeans missing in the recent Nepal flash floods, some social media posts started that they were “not our own” because most of those missing were ethnic Indians. One post even referred to them as “ABNN,” a derogatory term for Indians. Temasek chief executive Dilhan Pillay Sandrasegara, who is of Indian origin, was similarly attacked after Air India announced that it was seeking fresh capital from its shareholders.

articles.title: Al-Qaida: 25 Years After 9/11
articles.excerpt: Twenty-five years after the fateful terrorist attacks on the World Trade Center and the Pentagon on September 11, 2001, the fraternity of terrorism scholars and practitioners is divided over al-Qaida’s status. Some believe that al-Qaida still poses a potent threat to global peace and security, albeit of a different nature, while others think it has lost its mojo. Indeed, al-Qaida failed to create the Sunni global Caliphate it promised its followers. In fact, the global jihadist movement split between al-Qaida and the Islamic State (IS), which weakened the former. IS has superseded al-Qaida as the dominant global jihadist actor. The ideological tussle and inter-group fighting between al-Qaida and IS have helped security and intelligence agencies around the world to cut them to size. The strategic defeat that al-Qaida desperately wanted to inflict upon the United States has not materialized. Indubitably, the U.S. is struggling to retain its global hegemony in the face of China’s meteoric rise, but it is for a different set of reasons. Attributing power challenges to the U.S.-led unipolar system to al-Qaida would be a gross exaggeration and distortion of facts. In terrorism, violence is the central benchmark of evaluating the success or failure of a terrorist group. Al-Qaida Core, operating out of Afghanistan, has not carried out an international terrorist attack in more than a decade. The majority of al-Qaida’s top leaders, barring the current de facto chief Saif al-Adel and his deputy Abd al-Rahman al-Maghrebi, have been eliminated by the U.S. in drone strikes and targeted assassinations. Saif al-Adel likely lives in a safe house in Iran and is dependent on Iranian intelligence for his own security. This has undermined his credibility and capacity to command loyalty and obedience from various al-Qaida affiliates.

articles.title: Vietnam’s To Lam Concludes State Visit to Russia, Departs For France
articles.excerpt: Vietnam’s top leader To Lam yesterday wound up a state visit to Russia during which he and Russian President Vladimir Putin pledged to develop their cooperation in the realms of trade, energy, and defense. Lam arrived in Russia on Monday for a three-day visit, before departing yesterday for France, where he was scheduled to meet with President Emmanuel Macron and attend the International Space Summit in Paris. During the visit, Lam, who serves both as president and general secretary of the Communist Party of Vietnam (CPV), held talks with Putin, Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin, Chairman of the State Duma Vyacheslav Volodin, and other high-ranking officials. Ahead of their meeting, Putin praised Vietnam’s “impressive results” under the CPV’s rule, and said that he was “delighted” to welcome Lam and his delegation to the Kremlin. In turn, the Vietnamese leader described Putin as “a great friend of our country,” and said that Hanoi views its relationship with Moscow as “a priority, a consistent pillar of our foreign policy, and a strategic choice of enduring significance.” Both sides made ample reference to the Cold War-era cooperation between communist North Vietnam and the Soviet Union. Addressing the media after the meeting, Putin described the talks as “very meaningful and substantive” and said that the two sides had signed an “impressive package” of bilateral agreements. These included MoUs in areas such as justice, finance, investment, transport, ethnic affairs, energy, nuclear safety, science and technology, education, and mineral resources, Vietnamese state media reported. Putin said that economics and trade was a particular focus of talks.

articles.title: Is Indonesia’s 100 GW Solar Plan Realistic?
articles.excerpt: Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto has set an extremely ambitious target of building 100 GW of solar capacity by 2029. Naturally, many people are wondering if this a realistic goal. I’ll spare you the suspense. The answer is no. But it does send a strong signal that the government is serious about putting more resources toward cleaner energy. People often look at Indonesia’s energy sector, dominated by coal and other fossil fuels, and the extremely slow progress on renewables to date, and conclude that clean energy is a non-starter. I don’t agree. The government has been signaling for some time that it is willing to pivot toward clean energy. The catch is that it wants to do so on its own terms, without simply opening Indonesia up as a market for private developers and investors where the state-owned utility PLN ends up on the hook for expensive purchase agreements. This, in my estimation, was the major flaw with how Indonesia’s Just Energy Transition Partnership was originally designed. The actually important question is not whether Indonesia can build 100 GW of solar power – obviously, it cannot do so in three years. The question is whether we are getting closer to an approach that can actually be implemented and scaled given the peculiarities of Indonesia’s political economy. I think the answer is a tentative yes. Prabowo recently unveiled the first stage of the 100 GW plan, announcing 5.3 GW of solar power projects under development or which will soon be opened for bidding. The first thing we need to do is unpack the headline figure. 5.3 GW of new solar capacity would be a very significant step forward in Indonesia’s clean energy ambitions, but only eight of these projects are actually in an advanced stage of development. The bulk of the announced capacity, some 4.5 GW worth of projects, are still in the early stages without financing or confirmed project developers.

articles.title: El Niño, Climate Catastrophe, and the Coming Financial Showdown
articles.excerpt: Beyond the Mekong | Environment | Southeast Asia Pablo Berrutti discusses Nepal’s glacial collapse, Indonesia’s wildfires, and why efforts at climate mitigation are falling short. Mud covers buildings and properties following devastating floods in Trishuli, Nuwakot District, Nepal, Aug. 27, 2026. Credit: Shutterstock Pablo Berrutti is founder and managing director of Altiorem, a sustainable finance library, and a strategic advisor with a background in the integration of artificial intelligence, measuring the impact of climate change and its impact on business. This includes banks and insurance companies and their awkward relationships with factoring in the challenges of climate change and confronting their responsibilities, which have recently been sorely tested by the arrival of a super-charged El Niño weather phenomena. In recent weeks the glacial collapse in Nepal, wildfires in Indonesia, the haze, droughts, and typhoons across East Asia have taken horrible toll on human life and racked up damage bills that will be measured in the tens of billions of dollars. Governments and financial institutions were warned. The potential for this year’s El Niño was first raised in May and formally announced on June 16. The World Meteorological Organization says the current conditions are expected to last until February. But Berrutti told The Diplomat’s Luke Hunt that wealthy countries like Australia had spent very little on preparation and building in resilience into assets. Instead, about 95 percent of disaster funds went to recovery. “Whereas other countries, sadly, who aren’t as wealthy as Australia, a lot of Southeast Asian countries, clearly aren’t in a position to be able to build that resilience to these types of events,” he said. He added that it’s not only the big events that made headlines for causing destruction and loss of life that matter, but also the chronic effects of extreme heat. More than 30,000 people had died this year from back-to-back European heatwaves.

articles.title: Philippine Court Acquits Former First Lady Imelda Marcos of Corruption
articles.excerpt: The Philippine Supreme Court yesterday overturned a corruption conviction against Imelda Marcos, the mother of President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., more than three decades after the initial charges were filed. In November 2018, the Sandiganbayan, the Philippines’ special anti-corruption court, convicted the former first lady, now 97, of seven counts of graft and sentenced her to sentenced her six to 11 years imprisonment for each charge. It also barred her from holding political office for life. In a decision dated June 10 but made public yesterday, the 1st Division of the Supreme Court overturned the Sandiganbayan’s ruling, Rappler reported. In a 50-page ruling, Associate Justice Rodil Zalameda said that the prosecution had failed to prove her guilt “beyond reasonable doubt” and said that the key testimony and documentary evidence used against her were “inadmissible and lacked sufficient probative weight.” The cases stemmed from allegations that Marcos and her late husband, deposed President Ferdinand Marcos Sr., used a network of Swiss foundations to hold and transfer at least $200 million abroad during her 1975-1986 term as Manila governor. The Supreme Court decision did not dispute that the transactions had taken place, but ruled that the prosecution failed to meet the evidentiary requirements necessary to sustain criminal convictions.

articles.title: North Korea’s Nicaragua Courtship
articles.excerpt: Since emerging from its self-imposed COVID-19 isolation, North Korea has closed a number of its diplomatic missions overseas while reshaping others. The government has concentrated on relationships it sees as strategically useful, focusing heavily on deepening ties with Russia, its burgeoning relations with Belarus, and, most recently, the rekindling of engagement with China. Yet, amid this diplomatic retrenchment, one unexpected country has received particular outreach and attention from the Kim Jong Un regime: Nicaragua. At a time when North Korea is restructuring its foreign relationships, its decision to court Nicaragua stands out, both for its geographic position and the fact that it came at the invitation of the Kim regime. While the two countries seem like natural partners given the nature of their authoritarian systems of government and long-standing history, the outreach is nevertheless a notable deviation from North Korea’s baseline behavior. Ultimately it could signal increased cooperation between the two countries as well a new trajectory for North Korea’s foreign policy designs going forward, one that exists outside China’s and Russia’s immediate orbit. Background on the Nicaragua-North Korea relationship North Korea’s relationship with Nicaragua has ebbed and flowed with changes in Managua’s government. Pyongyang avoided diplomatic relations with the U.S.-backed Nicaraguan government until 1979, when the Sandinista National Liberation Front took power. At the time, the Kim regime’s connections to the Sandinistas largely ran through its Cuban partner, although North Korea had reportedly provided military training to the group’s personnel in the lead-up to the revolution. Bilateral engagement between the two countries peaked in the 1980s. This included North Korean military assistance with the delivery of four patrol vessels valued at $8 million, as well as mutual diplomatic support.

articles.title: Shifting Poles and Power 35 Years After the End of the Soviet Union
articles.excerpt: Since late August, seven of the 15 republics of the former Soviet Union celebrated the 35th anniversary of the declaration of their independence. Some marked the occasion in spectacular fashion, such as Uzbekistan and others with more sedate celebrations. But all sought to display and embrace the national identities they have developed since attaining sovereignty. In 1991, the Soviet Union collapsed and the bipolar world of the time came to an end. In the post-Cold War period, widely described as a period of U.S. unipolarity, when there was no power that could seriously challenge U.S. supremacy, the new republics worked hard to strengthen their national identities. The rise of China, and Russia’s resurgence under President Vladimir Putin, changed the balance of power in the late 2000s. Today, the dominant narrative – not only in countries of the Global South in general and in the post-Soviet space in particular but increasingly in Western discourse, too – is that the world is shifting toward a different system, a multipolar one. This multipolarity is on display across the post-Soviet space. The Baltic states, for example, became NATO members in the early 2000s. In Eastern Europe, while Belarus became a close ally of Russia, Ukraine hedged and then inched toward the West. In Russian discourse, Ukraine’s desire to join NATO was a threat to Moscow’s security. Other states in the South Caucasus and Central Asia continue to hedge among the various poles in the emerging multipolar world. What does security look like for the current post-Soviet states? Has the world indeed become multipolar for these states or has it been multipolar for them all along?

articles.title: North Korean Elites and Regime Weakness
articles.excerpt: The Diplomat author Mercy Kuo regularly engages subject-matter experts, policy practitioners, and strategic thinkers across the globe for their diverse insights into U.S. Asia policy. This conversation with Dr. Jieun Baek – author of “Privileged but Powerless: How North Korean Elite Grievances Reveal the Regime’s Greatest Weakness” (Yale 2026) – is the 525th in “The Trans-Pacific View Insight Series.” Describe the key characteristics of North Korea’s elites. North Korea officially rejects the idea that it has an elite class, yet it is one of the world’s most stratified societies. Its elites include Korean Workers’ Party cadres, intellectuals, senior military and security officials, and individuals personally close to Kim Jong Un. The traditional elite largely inherits status through favorable songbun [North Korea’s hierarchical classification system], family history, and proven political loyalty. A newer unofficial elite – the donju, or “masters of money” – derives influence from capital, markets, and connections. These groups are not monolithic, but they share one defining characteristic: their positions help maintain the regime. In return, they may receive Pyongyang residency, superior housing and education, better food, prestigious employment and education, overseas opportunities, and access to luxury goods – European watches, imported cosmetics, pet poodles. None of this is discreet. The regime stages elite reward deliberately. When the Kyongru-dong neighborhood opened, officials framed the new housing not as a public good but as the deserved inheritance of those whose loyalty had earned them “the best of civilization.” Yet every privilege is conditional. Elites must continuously demonstrate political reliability, professional usefulness, and personal loyalty to Kim. And the most privileged are also the most closely watched: privilege and surveillance rise together.

articles.title: The Ultimate Hedger: Why Vietnam Is Thriving Amid Global Disorder
articles.excerpt: Vietnam has emerged as a leading strategic hedger in a global order undergoing major power transition. In other words, it has engaged in “repeated, diverse, sustained, and complementary actions to engage with all major powers without reaching a formal alliance with any and without restrictions on possible actions with others.” On April 2, 2025, Vietnam’s strategy faced a massive test: on so-called “Liberation Day,” U.S. President Donald Trump targeted Vietnam with a punishing 46 percent tariff, accusing the country of conniving with China on transshipment and treating the United States unfairly. Totaling $123.5 billion, the U.S. trade deficit with Vietnam was the third largest after its deficits with China and Mexico. It attracted attention. On April 14-15, Chinese President Xi Jinping was in Hanoi, pressuring Vietnam not to give in too much to the United States. With pressure from both sides, the future of Vietnam as a connector country in global supply chains was under great stress. Fast forward 16 months, and Vietnam has not just survived in the disorder; it has thrived. Overall exports increased by 17 percent in 2025 overall (and exports to the U.S. increased 28 percent, to $153 billion). In the first seven months of 2026, the U.S. imported $104.7 billion worth of goods from Vietnam, a 23 percent year-on-year increase. Vietnam’s GDP growth rate reached 8 percent in 2025 and 8.18 percent in the first half of 2026, despite trade tensions and the Iran war, and in contrast to the prediction of 5.6 percent for 2025 made by the IMF Outlook in September 2025. To accomplish this economic feat, Vietnam did not throw its lot in with one great power or join an alliance. In fact, it doubled down in its strategic behavior as a hedger. Vietnam is deeply committed, for strategic and historic reasons, to respond to uncertainty and global geopolitical tensions by hedging. Amazingly, it has worked so far.

articles.title: Russia Is Helping Supercharge North Korea’s Military Drones
articles.excerpt: Russia’s expanding military partnership with North Korea has become one of the most significant proliferation risks of the Ukraine war. Since Pyongyang began actively supporting Russia’s campaign, Moscow is believed to have transferred sensitive technologies such as naval reactors for nuclear‑powered submarines, air defense systems, and other advanced capabilities in exchange for North Korean weapons and troops. Russia has already provided drone technology to Pyongyang, and the rapid evolution of Russian battlefield innovations now raises concerns that North Korea could, in time, gain access to far more sophisticated systems, including new versions of autonomous AI–enabled and jet–powered drones. In a war that began as an artillery‑heavy conflict, drone usage and tactics have evolved rapidly. One of the most consequential developments is Russia’s experimentation with autonomously controlled AI‑enabled drones. Earlier iterations required a human operator to confirm targets, with AI used primarily to counter radio‑jamming and ensure the drone reached its destination. In recent months, however, Russia has begun allowing onboard AI systems to make independent strike decisions. This shift toward autonomous targeting represents a significant technological leap and raises concerns that North Korea, already receiving Russian drone technology, could eventually gain access to these more advanced capabilities. As with much of the evolution of technology in the Ukraine war, Russia’s has equipped its autonomous AI drones with off-the-shelf technology, specifically commercial grade Nvidia Jetson Orin computers designed to create AI-enabled devices. Using such tools, Russia is training the drone AI to identify specific targets such as gas stations. Russia has also begun modifying drones with jet powered engines. Jet powered drones are more expensive than the propellor powered models that have been heavily utilized during the war, but they are also more difficult to shoot down.

articles.title: IA : le patron d’Anthropic, Dario Amodei, appelle à ralentir la vitesse de développement de l’intelligence artificielle avant que des agents soient « capables de prendre le contrôle d’internet »
articles.excerpt: Pixels Pixels Intelligence artificielle Intelligence artificielle Intelligence artificielle Le message publié samedi par Dario Amodei survient quelques jours après qu’un chercheur d’Anthropic, Jacob Coxon, a annoncé quitter la start-up californienne, l’accusant de minimiser le risque existentiel que présente l’IA pour l’humanité. Le patron d’Anthropic, Dario Amodei, a appelé samedi 12 septembre à ralentir la vitesse de développement de l’intelligence artificielle (IA), évoquant la nécessité de mieux contrôler ses évolutions et l’incident survenu en juillet chez OpenAI. Il faut « temporiser » l’amélioration de l’IA « pour que la prévention des risques soit en mesure de suivre le rythme », a écrit le directeur général d’Anthropic dans un message publié sur son site personnel. Dario Amodei fait écho à un autre appel, lancé au début de juin par Anthropic, à donner la possibilité aux grands acteurs de l’IA de « ralentir ou suspendre temporairement le développement » de cette technologie. A la fin de juillet, Sam Altman, patron de son grand rival OpenAI, avait, à son tour, parlé de lever le pied « pour donner suffisamment de temps à la société de faire face à ces nouvelles capacités ». Dans la foulée, plus d’un millier d’employés d’entreprises à la pointe de l’IA, y compris Dario Amodei et des dirigeants d’OpenAI, avaient demandé au gouvernement américain d’aider à « temporiser » la sortie des modèles les plus avancés. Ces exhortations avaient lieu après un incident lors duquel des modèles d’OpenAI étaient sortis spontanément de leur milieu confiné au cours de tests pour rejoindre Internet et attaquer la plateforme d’IA Hugging Face. « Des centaines de milliards de dollars de dégâts » Depuis, plusieurs autres événements ayant vu des intelligences artificielles d’OpenAI et Anthropic se rendre sur Internet à l’insu de leurs superviseurs ont été rapportés par les deux entreprises.

articles.title: Céline Dion feiert emotionales Comeback
articles.excerpt: Mit Tränen in den Augen hat Weltstar Céline Dion vor Zehntausenden Fans ihr Bühnen-Comeback hingelegt. Die 58-jährige Kanadierin sang zum Auftakt ihres ersten Konzerts nach sechs Jahren Pause »On Ne Change Pas« (Auf Deutsch: Man ändert sich nicht). Die Sängerin war sichtlich gerührt und wischte sich Tränen aus dem Gesicht. »Ich hatte mir versprochen, nicht zu weinen«, sagte Dion. Doch dieses Versprechen halte sie nun nicht ein. In der ausverkauften Plenitude Arena in Nanterre bei Paris sagte die Musikerin: »Heute Abend will ich für euch singen, für mich singen, das Leben besingen.« Auch aus Deutschland und Österreich reisten Anhänger der Sängerin an.In den vergangenen Jahren war Dion nur noch selten aufgetreten. Die Sängerin leidet am Stiff-Person-Syndrom. Muskeln, Sehnen und Nerven lassen sich dabei zeitweise nicht mehr kontrollieren. 17 Jahre verbarg Dion ihre Autoimmunerkrankung. 2021 waren die Symptome jedoch so schwer, dass sie ihre Konzerte absagen musste – und ein Jahr später ihre Diagnose öffentlich machte. Ihre Stimme entglitt ihr, zeitweilig konnte sie ihr Haus kaum mehr verlassen.Wegen der Erkrankung hing es jeweils von ihrer Tagesform ab, ob sie verreisen oder auf der Bühne singen konnte. Im Frühjahr hatte sie dann ihre Rückkehr auf die Konzertbühne angekündigt. »Ich fühle mich gut, ich bin stark, ich bin aufgeregt, natürlich ein bisschen nervös, aber vor allem bin ich euch allen sehr dankbar!«, hatte sie gesagt.

articles.title: Ebola: Mehr als 7000 Fälle in Demokratischer Republik Kongo erfasst
articles.excerpt: Experten gehen von einer hohen Zahl nicht erfasster Fälle aus, zudem werden nur die Fälle seit Bekanntgabe des Ausbruchs am 15. Mai erfasst. Vermutet wird, dass der Ausbruch zuvor schon monatelang unerkannt lief.Von den 7022 registrierten Erkrankten starben den Behörden zufolge 3398. Derzeit befänden sich 837 Menschen in Isolation oder Behandlung. Erstmals wurde ein Fall in der Provinz Süd-Ubangi im Nordwesten des Landes nachgewiesen. Es handelt sich um die siebte betroffene Provinz. Der Ausbruch hatte im Osten des zweitgrößten afrikanischen Landes begonnen.Auch der Anstieg der Todesfälle habe sich etwas verlangsamt – vermutlich, weil mehr Menschen frühzeitig Behandlungszentren aufsuchten. Allerdings sei die Zahl der Menschen, die außerhalb der Behandlungszentren in ihren Dörfern oder normalen Krankenhäusern sterben, noch immer zu hoch. Ebolafieber ist eine lebensbedrohliche Krankheit. Das Virus wird durch Körperkontakt und Kontakt mit Körperflüssigkeiten übertragen und löst ein hochansteckendes Fieber mit Durchfall und Blutungen aus. Der aktuelle Ausbruch ist besonders schwer einzudämmen, auch weil es für den Ebola-Erreger vom Typ Bundibugyo bislang weder einen speziellen Impfstoff noch eine spezielle Therapie gibt.
articles.summary: 专家认为未记录在案的病例数量很高，而且只统计了自5月15日宣布疫情暴发以来的病例。据推测，疫情此前已悄无声息地持续了数月。当局称，在登记的7022名感染者中，已有3398人死亡。目前有837人处于隔离或治疗之中。该国西北部的南乌班吉省首次发现一例病例，这是受影响的第七个省份。此次疫情始于这个非洲第二大国的东部。死亡人数的增长速度也有所放缓——可能因为更多人及早前往治疗中心就诊。不过，在治疗中心之外、在村庄或普通医院中死亡的人数仍然过高。埃博拉热是一种危及生命的疾病。该病毒通过身体接触和接触体液传播，会引发伴有腹泻和出血的高传染性发热。当前这轮疫情尤其难以遏制，部分原因在于针对本迪布焦型埃博拉病毒，迄今既没有专门的疫苗，也没有专门的治疗方法。

articles.title: Ermittler sehen bei Zugunglück in Frankreich keine Hinweise auf Anschlag
articles.excerpt: Nach dem Entgleisen eines Regionalzugs in Nordwestfrankreich mit 44 Verletzten gehen die Ermittler nach derzeitigen Erkenntnissen nicht von einem Anschlag aus. »Es gibt keinerlei Anhaltspunkte, die auf einen Anschlag hindeuten«, erklärte am Samstag der Staatsanwalt von Rouen, Sébastien Gallois. Politiker hatten zuvor von einem »kriminellen Akt« oder einem »Attentat« gesprochen. Der TER-Regionalzug mit 186 Passagieren war am Freitagabend in der Normandie zwischen den Städten Rouen und Caen unterwegs gewesen, als er nahe Cléon entgleiste. Auf der Strecke sei ein Schienenteil gefunden worden, erklärte Staatsanwalt Gallois. Die Gründe dafür müssten im Rahmen einer Untersuchung geklärt werden. Es gebe aber bisher keine »Anhaltspunkte für eine böswillige Handlung und schon gar nicht für einen Anschlag«. Der rechtsgerichtete Bürgermeister von Nizza, Eric Ciotti, hatte zuvor erklärt, die Entgleisung des Zugs sei »das Ergebnis eines Anschlags«. Er forderte, dass die Täter »mit größter Entschiedenheit« bestraft werden. Unfallstelle nahe Cléon: »Es war wirklich schockierend« Foto: Fourmy Mario / ABACAPRESS / IMAGO Der Präsident der Region Normandie, Hervé Morin, sagte, es sei von einem »kriminellen Akt« auszugehen. Das 250 bis 300 Kilogramm schwere Schienenstück sei nicht »einfach so auf die Gleise gelangt«. Eine Stunde vor der Entgleisung des Zugs sei an der betreffenden Stelle ein Zug vorbeigefahren und in der Zwischenzeit hätten dort keine Bauarbeiten stattgefunden. Der 24-jährige Fahrgast Louis beschrieb im Radiosender Ici Normandie, er habe kurz vor dem Entgleisen des Zugs ein Ruckeln gespürt, das immer stärker geworden sei. Dann habe er sich nicht auf seinem Sitz halten können. »Die Fenster sind teilweise zerborsten, die Steine vom Gleisbett flogen in den Waggon. Es war wirklich schockierend«, sagte er. Unter den 44 Verletzten befindet sich eine 18-Jährige, deren Zustand die Behörden zunächst als »kritisch« bezeichneten.

articles.title: Donald Trumps Elternhaus für zwei Millionen US-Dollar verkauft
articles.excerpt: Das Elternhaus von Präsident Donald Trump in New York ist für fast zwei Millionen Dollar verkauft worden. Das zuvor leerstehende und vernachlässigte Gebäude war vor dem Verkauf saniert worden.Der Präsident lebte bis zu seinem vierten Lebensjahr in dem im Tudor-Stil erbauten Anwesen in Queens. Sein Vater, der Bauunternehmer Fred Trump, hatte das Haus 1940 im wohlhabenden Stadtteil Jamaica Estates erbaut. Die Familie ist schon seit Jahren nicht mehr Eigentümerin des Hauses. Der Verkaufspreis von 1,93 Millionen Dollar wurde am Freitag auf Immobilien-Websites veröffentlicht, nachdem ein Käufer, dessen Name nicht bekannt gegeben wurde, im Juli einen Vertrag abgeschlossen hatte. Wohnzimmer in Trumps Elternhaus (Aufnahme aus dem Oktober 2016) Foto: AP Der Verkäufer Tommy Lin hatte das Haus mit fünf Schlafzimmern und drei Bädern im vergangenen Jahr für 835.000 Dollar erworben. Es stand jahrelang leer und war vernachlässigt worden.Lin, der als Bauträger arbeitet, gab weitere 500.000 Dollar für eine achtmonatige Innenrenovierung aus. Dabei wurden Annehmlichkeiten wie eine Profiküche, Fischgrätenparkett und Badezimmer im Spa-Stil hinzugefügt, wie die »New York Post« berichtet. Das Haus hat in den vergangenen Jahren mehrfach den Besitzer gewechselt, unter anderem für 2,14 Millionen Dollar wenige Monate nach Trumps Amtsantritt als Präsident im Jahr 2017, wie aus Daten des Immobilienvermittlers Zillow hervorgeht. Schlafzimmer in Trumps Elternhaus (Aufnahme aus dem Oktober 2016) Foto: Mary Altaffer/ AP Käufer war eine Gesellschaft namens »Trump Birth Home LLC«. Das Haus wurde kurzzeitig auf Airbnb zur Vermietung angeboten – komplett mit Kopien einer lebensgroßen Pappfigur von Trump, Exemplaren seines Buches »The Art of the Deal« und einem gerahmten Titelblatt des People-Magazins mit Trump. Im Jahr 2019 wurde es erneut zum Verkauf angeboten, diesmal mit einer Preisvorstellung von 2,9 Millionen Dollar.

articles.title: OpenAI verschiebt Börsengang wegen Sicherheitsbedenken
articles.excerpt: OpenAI-Chef Sam Altman Foto: Kim Kyung-Hoon / REUTERS Der mit Spannung erwartete Börsengang des ChatGPT-Entwicklers OpenAI wird in diesem Jahr nach Angaben von Firmenchef Sam Altman nicht mehr über die Bühne gehen. Er verwies in einem Interview des Magazins »Fortune« auf die aktuelle Debatte über die Gefahren hoch entwickelter künstlicher Intelligenz. »Man wäre schlecht beraten, genau jetzt an die Börse zu gehen«, sagte Altman. Auf die Nachfrage, ob er sich auch den Verzicht auf einen Börsengang im kommenden Jahr vorstellen könnte, erwiderte Altman: »Ich würde sagen, nicht 2026.« ChatGPT löste vor mehreren Jahren den anhaltenden Hype um künstliche Intelligenz aus. OpenAI dürfte beim Börsengang nicht nur Dutzende Milliarden Dollar einnehmen, sondern auch eine sehr hohe Bewertung erzielen. Die Aktienplatzierung wird schon länger geplant.KI-Forscher warnen vor künstlicher IntelligenzSeit Wochen gibt es große Sorgen um Risiken künstlicher Intelligenz. Sie wurden von Hacking-Attacken durch KI-Software ausgelöst, die sich in Testläufen selbstständig gemacht hatte. In den vergangenen Tagen wurde die Debatte über KI-Sicherheit zusätzlich von dem Forscher Jacob Coxon angeheizt. Er arbeitete für die KI-Firma Anthropic und trat mit einer drastischen Warnung zurück: Die großen Entwickler künstlicher Intelligenz handelten unverantwortlich »und spielen mit unseren Leben«, betonte Coxon. Anthropic-Forscher Evan Hubinger, der mit dafür zuständig ist, dass KI mit den Interessen der Menschen im Einklang bleibt, bestätigte wenig später Coxons Sorgen. Er persönlich denke, die Gefahr, dass KI die Menschheit töte, liege im kommenden Jahrzehnt bei mehr als zehn Prozent, schrieb er auf der Onlineplattform X.
